title: The Royal Society: a journal outlives its founder
question: What lets an intellectual network become a durable institution?
summary: Henry Oldenburg began Philosophical Transactions in 1665 as a personal publishing venture within the Royal Society’s scientific network. Individual successors continued the journal before the Society took responsibility in 1752. Its survival depended on recurring work: selecting papers, maintaining correspondence, editing issues, and finding money to publish them.
outcome_summary: A durable publication and scientific institution emerged, but through repeated changes rather than an unchanged founding design. Survival did not mean commercial self-sufficiency: publishing drew on support for much of its history.

sections.title: What happened
sections.html:
Bounded success. A durable publication and scientific institution emerged, but through repeated changes rather than an unchanged founding design. Survival did not mean commercial self-sufficiency: publishing drew on support for much of its history.

  • The Royal Society formed in 1660 and received a royal charter in 1662. History of the Royal Society
  • Oldenburg launched Philosophical Transactions in 1665; the Society assumed responsibility in 1752. History of Philosophical Transactions
  • Reviewing and publication arrangements changed over time. Publishing cost the Society more than it earned during the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. History of Philosophical Transactions Journals, learned societies and money: Philosophical Transactions, ca. 1750–1900

sections.title: What might explain it
sections.html:
Plausible

Royal recognition helped make the network legitimate and attractive. Great Founder Theory — 2020 manuscript History of the Royal Society

Alternative explanation: Correspondence, experiments and useful publications may have mattered more to participants than royal prestige.

Supported in case

Transferring recurring editorial and financial work to an organization helped continuity. History of Philosophical Transactions Journals, learned societies and money: Philosophical Transactions, ca. 1750–1900

Alternative explanation: Individual successors had already kept the journal alive before the Society took ownership; organizational ownership was one stage in a longer process.

sections.title: Understanding the outcome
sections.html:
Institutionalization and knowledge succession

A journal can preserve a founder’s purpose only if later people can inherit the work, contacts, budget, and authority needed to keep publishing. The name and prestige alone do not perform those tasks. Great Founder Theory — 2020 manuscript History of Philosophical Transactions

The Royal Society had unusually durable recognition and support. A new journal without those resources faces a different succession problem.

sections.title: Questions to take into practice
sections.html:
• Who will perform the recurring maintenance after the founder leaves?
  • Can recognition attract resources without substituting for substantive evaluation?

sections.title: What remains uncertain
sections.html: • How much did royal recognition contribute to the journal’s survival compared with its scientific usefulness and financial support? Its long history also leaves a separate question about who could participate and whose work was excluded.

title: Lysenkoism: when authority can overrule evidence
question: What happens when scientific standing depends on political loyalty?
summary: Lysenko’s rise joined political sponsorship to control of scientific appointments and institutions. The 1948 academy session made opposition to established genetics official policy. This is a case of organizational power suppressing correction, rather than merely a scientist holding a mistaken theory.
outcome_summary: Political intervention suppressed geneticists and damaged scientific institutions. Reversing official doctrine did not immediately restore the people, appointments, and research traditions that had been disrupted.

sections.title: What happened
sections.html:
Failure on the stated objective. Political intervention suppressed geneticists and damaged scientific institutions. Reversing official doctrine did not immediately restore the people, appointments, and research traditions that had been disrupted.

  • Stalin-backed intervention at the 1948 academy session prohibited genetics research and promoted Lysenko’s position. Lysenkoism Against Genetics: The Meeting of August 1948, Its Background, Causes, and Aftermath
  • Research traditions were interrupted as geneticists and institutions came under political pressure. Lysenkoism Against Genetics: The Meeting of August 1948, Its Background, Causes, and Aftermath
  • Institutional arrangements associated with Lysenkoism persisted beyond the rejection of its scientific claims, complicating recovery. Lysenko Unemployed: Soviet Genetics after the Aftermath

sections.title: What might explain it
sections.html:
Supported in case

Political control made scientific disagreement costly and helped shield favored claims from correction. Lysenkoism Against Genetics: The Meeting of August 1948, Its Background, Causes, and Aftermath

Alternative explanation: Career competition, economic pressures and institutional rivalry also contributed; political ideology alone is incomplete.

Plausible

Changing official doctrine is insufficient if appointments and institutional dependencies persist. Lysenko Unemployed: Soviet Genetics after the Aftermath

Alternative explanation: Recovery may also have been slowed by the loss of trained people and interrupted research, even where appointments or rules had changed.

sections.title: Understanding the outcome
sections.html:
Capture and suppression of error correction

When the authority judging a scientific claim also controls the careers of its critics, a mistaken claim can survive challenges that would otherwise expose it. Lysenkoism Against Genetics: The Meeting of August 1948, Its Background, Causes, and Aftermath Lysenko Unemployed: Soviet Genetics after the Aftermath

The decisive feature here was repression of criticism. Disagreement about research priorities is a different situation unless comparable control over dissent is present.

sections.title: Questions to take into practice
sections.html:
• Can evidence overturn the claim of a powerful sponsor?
  • What happens to a dissenter’s job, access and ability to publish?

sections.title: What remains uncertain
sections.html: • How much did the later recovery depend on changes in appointments, protection for criticism, or rebuilding research networks? Those processes need to be distinguished from the formal rejection of Lysenko’s ideas.

sections.title: Sources
sections.html: • Great Founder Theory — 2020 manuscript — Samo Burja

title: The Manhattan Project: coordination at enormous human cost
question: Can mission achievement be separated from the legitimacy and costs of the mission?
summary: The Manhattan Project coordinated scientific teams, public resources, contractors, and large sites under wartime military authority to develop atomic weapons. Its leaders could mobilize resources on an extraordinary scale. The same authority could impose decisions on people outside the project, including communities displaced to make room for its facilities.
outcome_summary: The project achieved its weapons-development objective. That technical achievement came with destructive consequences and costs borne by people who did not choose the mission, including displacement at Oak Ridge.

sections.title: What happened
sections.html:
Mixed outcomes. The project achieved its weapons-development objective. That technical achievement came with destructive consequences and costs borne by people who did not choose the mission, including displacement at Oak Ridge.

  • General Leslie Groves’s responsibilities included obtaining resources, recruiting expertise, and selecting project sites. Manhattan Project Site Selection
  • Acquiring the Oak Ridge site displaced existing rural communities. Oak Ridge: Displacement

sections.title: What might explain it
sections.html:
Plausible

A clear mandate and concentrated authority reduced some coordination and resource-allocation obstacles. Manhattan Project Site Selection Great Founder Theory — 2020 manuscript

Alternative explanation: Exceptional wartime funding, urgency and accumulated scientific knowledge may explain much of the speed.

Plausible

Secrecy and administrative power shifted important costs onto people unable to contest the mission. Oak Ridge: Displacement

Alternative explanation: Urgency, the scale of the facilities, and the site chosen may have contributed to displacement alongside the project’s secrecy and concentrated authority.

sections.title: Understanding the outcome
sections.html:
Mission-oriented coordination

Technical leadership needed political authorization and access to resources. Concentrating those powers also limited the ability of affected communities to challenge decisions. Manhattan Project Site Selection Great Founder Theory — 2020 manuscript

Wartime authority and exceptional public funding changed which actions were possible and who could contest them. A civilian project must establish its mandate and accountability under different conditions.

sections.title: Questions to take into practice
sections.html:
• Whose definition of success is being used?
  • Can a project secure resources while preserving challenge and accountability?

sections.title: What remains uncertain
sections.html: • How much of the project’s speed came from its authority structure, and how much from exceptional funding, urgency, and prior scientific work? The experience of displaced residents and workers also matters when judging what the organizational achievement cost.

title: Apollo: a clear goal still needed a coalition
question: What makes a large mission survive beyond the person who announced it?
summary: Apollo combined a public deadline with contractors, administrative coordination and continuing political support. A successful landing depended on more than an inspiring goal or one exceptional engineer. The case examines how a coalition can sustain a bounded mission while remaining vulnerable to changing priorities afterward.
outcome_summary: Apollo achieved the lunar landing in 1969, within the decade set by the 1961 goal. Its coalition sustained a specific mission; continuing a program afterward required renewed agreement about its purpose and cost.

sections.title: What happened
sections.html:
Bounded success. Apollo achieved the lunar landing in 1969, within the decade set by the 1961 goal. Its coalition sustained a specific mission; continuing a program afterward required renewed agreement about its purpose and cost.

  • Apollo achieved the 1969 landing within the goal announced in 1961. Managing America to the Moon: A Coalition Analysis
  • The mission depended on cooperation across technical teams, administrators, contractors, and political supporters. Managing America to the Moon: A Coalition Analysis
  • NASA coordinated extensive contracted work rather than producing the entire system in-house. Apollo: A Retrospective Analysis

sections.title: What might explain it
sections.html:
Supported in case

A shared concrete objective helped align institutions with different interests. Managing America to the Moon: A Coalition Analysis

Alternative explanation: Cold War competition and exceptional public expenditure also supplied commitment.

Plausible

Contracting let NASA combine dispersed capabilities while retaining systems-level integration. Apollo: A Retrospective Analysis

Alternative explanation: The ability to integrate contractors may have mattered more than contracting itself; distributing work can also fragment accountability.

sections.title: Understanding the outcome
sections.html:
Coalition analysis of program implementation

A deadline coordinates work only while people with different responsibilities continue to supply decisions, funding, and capabilities. Apollo’s coalition made the goal executable. Managing America to the Moon: A Coalition Analysis

The visibility and political urgency of a lunar landing helped mobilize resources that routine public services cannot assume.

sections.title: Questions to take into practice
sections.html:
• Which coalition will still support the project after its founder or political sponsor leaves?
  • Who integrates work across contractors and resolves tradeoffs?

sections.title: What remains uncertain
sections.html: • How much did the management arrangements contribute compared with Cold War priorities and exceptional expenditure? Achieving the deadline does not reveal what a different contracting or funding arrangement would have cost.

sections.title: Sources
sections.html: • Great Founder Theory — 2020 manuscript — Samo Burja

title: Challenger: warnings that did not reach the decision
question: How can an organization have expertise yet fail to use it?
summary: Before Challenger’s launch, engineers raised concerns that did not reach senior decision-makers intact. Management reversed an initial recommendation against launch, and the decision proceeded without key managers knowing the extent of the dispute. The failure was not simply a lack of expertise: the organization failed to carry that expertise into the decision.
outcome_summary: Challenger was lost and seven people died. The investigation identified failures in communication and management alongside the physical failure. Understanding the accident requires both the technical vulnerability and the process through which unresolved concerns were discounted.

sections.title: What happened
sections.html:
Failure on the stated objective. Challenger was lost and seven people died. The investigation identified failures in communication and management alongside the physical failure. Understanding the accident requires both the technical vulnerability and the process through which unresolved concerns were discounted.

  • The commission found incomplete or misleading information, conflict between engineering data and management judgments, and safety problems bypassing key managers. Report of the Presidential Commission on the Space Shuttle Challenger Accident, Volume 1
  • An initial recommendation against launch was reversed by management; senior managers were not aware of the dispute when the launch went ahead. Return to Flight: The Challenger Accident

sections.title: What might explain it
sections.html:
Supported in case

Escalation and decision procedures failed to preserve the substance of the engineering objection. Report of the Presidential Commission on the Space Shuttle Challenger Accident, Volume 1 Return to Flight: The Challenger Accident

Alternative explanation: The physical vulnerability and environmental conditions were necessary parts of the accident, not merely background.

Plausible

Organizational incentives may have made uncertain warnings easier to discount. Return to Flight: The Challenger Accident

Alternative explanation: Managers may have interpreted uncertain evidence through established routines as well as responding to organizational incentives. The decision record is needed to distinguish those influences.

sections.title: Understanding the outcome
sections.html:
Organizational error correction and voice

An objection can be raised yet fail to affect a decision if its content, uncertainty, or author’s judgment disappears during escalation. Having a reporting channel is different from preserving what it carries. Report of the Presidential Commission on the Space Shuttle Challenger Accident, Volume 1

A reporting procedure alone cannot be assumed to prevent accidents. Decision-makers also need authority, time, and a defined response to unresolved concerns.

sections.title: Questions to take into practice
sections.html:
• Can decision makers see the strongest unresolved objection in its author’s terms?
  • Who can pause the decision, and who owns the response to that pause?

sections.title: What remains uncertain
sections.html: • Why did the warnings lose force as they moved through the organization? Schedule pressures, accepted routines, and judgments about uncertain evidence may have contributed in different ways.

sections.title: Sources
sections.html: • Great Founder Theory — 2020 manuscript — Samo Burja

title: COTS: public capability helps build private capability
question: What does a market need before suppliers can finance delivery?
summary: NASA used milestone-based development partnerships to help firms build cargo transport capability. Firms retained substantial initiative, while NASA supplied funding, expertise, interfaces, and future demand. The program also ended a partnership when the supplier could not obtain financing, making both the support and the limits of the arrangement visible.
outcome_summary: SpaceX and Orbital completed demonstration missions; Rocketplane Kistler did not. Staged commitments produced working capability from some participants, but financing remained uncertain and negotiated service prices exceeded initial proposals.

sections.title: What happened
sections.html:
Mixed outcomes. SpaceX and Orbital completed demonstration missions; Rocketplane Kistler did not. Staged commitments produced working capability from some participants, but financing remained uncertain and negotiated service prices exceeded initial proposals.

  • SpaceX completed its COTS demonstration in 2012 and Orbital completed its demonstration in 2013. Commercial Orbital Transportation Services: A New Era in Spaceflight
  • NASA terminated Rocketplane Kistler after missed milestones; the oversight account records $32.1 million spent before termination. NASA’s Management of Commercial Orbital Transportation Services and ISS Commercial Resupply Contracts
  • Suppliers’ financing depended partly on credible future demand, and negotiated service prices grew beyond their initial proposals. Commercial Orbital Transportation Services: A New Era in Spaceflight

sections.title: What might explain it
sections.html:
Participant explanation

Staged payments and credible customer demand helped turn emerging capability into an investable undertaking. Commercial Orbital Transportation Services: A New Era in Spaceflight

Alternative explanation: Firm capability, founder capital and the availability of private finance also differed between participants.

Plausible

Terminating one partner and selecting another limited dependence on a single supplier. Commercial Orbital Transportation Services: A New Era in Spaceflight NASA’s Management of Commercial Orbital Transportation Services and ISS Commercial Resupply Contracts

Alternative explanation: The result could also reflect which firms were selected and what capabilities they already possessed; replacing a partner does not by itself explain overall program costs.

sections.title: Understanding the outcome
sections.html:
Complementarity of public procurement and entrepreneurial capacity

An emerging supplier needs more than a promising prototype. Funding, access to expertise, and a credible customer can make the next stage possible while leaving important risks with the firm. Commercial Orbital Transportation Services: A New Era in Spaceflight NASA’s Management of Commercial Orbital Transportation Services and ISS Commercial Resupply Contracts

Space transport combines unusually high entry costs with a small number of major customers. A market with many small buyers offers a different basis for financing.

sections.title: Questions to take into practice
sections.html:
• Does a supplier have a credible customer after the prototype?
  • What can be stopped or replaced without abandoning the entire mission?

sections.title: What remains uncertain
sections.html: • How would costs and delivery times have differed under another procurement arrangement? Comparing prototypes alone would miss later service prices, continuing public support, and the costs of unsuccessful participants.

sections.title: Sources
sections.html: • Great Founder Theory — 2020 manuscript — Samo Burja

title: Roman adoption: an heir is also a political alliance
question: How did adoption help an emperor establish a successor?
summary: Imperial adoption made selected adults members of a ruling family and recognizable successors. It could bring someone into the line of succession without making biological descent the only route. The selection still took place within elite family networks and political negotiations, rather than an open competition for the most capable ruler.
outcome_summary: Adoption helped establish recognizable succession arrangements, including the Antonine line. Naming an heir could coordinate expectations, but the heir still needed the support and resources required to govern.

sections.title: What happened
sections.html:
Mixed outcomes. Adoption helped establish recognizable succession arrangements, including the Antonine line. Naming an heir could coordinate expectations, but the heir still needed the support and resources required to govern.

  • Hadrian adopted Antoninus Pius, who adopted Marcus Aurelius and Lucius Verus. The Antonine Dynasty (138–193)
  • The Antonine dynasty drew on wealthy provincial and Italian family connections. The Antonine Dynasty (138–193)

sections.title: What might explain it
sections.html:
Plausible

Designating an heir could align the expectations of incumbent, successor and supporters. Great Founder Theory — 2020 manuscript The Antonine Dynasty (138–193)

Alternative explanation: Selection may instead ratify existing military and political power rather than create cooperation.

Plausible

Familiar family status helped make a negotiated succession socially intelligible. Great Founder Theory — 2020 manuscript

Alternative explanation: Legal adoption without elite acceptance would not guarantee a peaceful transfer.

sections.title: Understanding the outcome
sections.html:
Credible commitment and succession

Naming an heir gives supporters a person around whom to coordinate. Whether they actually accept the successor depends on relationships and resources beyond the legal designation. Great Founder Theory — 2020 manuscript An Emperor is Made: Senatorial Politics and Trajan’s Adoption by Nerva in 97

Succession within a restricted imperial elite differs from open hiring or democratic selection: the eligible candidates and the means of securing support were fundamentally different.

sections.title: Questions to take into practice
sections.html:
• Does naming a successor transfer informal support as well as a title?
  • Are apparent merit criteria explaining selection or rationalizing it afterward?

sections.title: What remains uncertain
sections.html: • How much did adoption itself secure cooperation, and how much did it formalize alliances that already existed? Military backing, family connections, and the exclusion of other candidates complicate any claim that the arrangement selected rulers by merit.

title: The Tetrarchy: a succession design that needed its designer
question: What breaks when a coordinating founder leaves?
summary: Diocletian divided rule among senior and junior emperors, combining present authority with an intended succession path. The arrangement addressed a vast empire’s coordination problem, yet its succession mechanism did not endure intact after retirement. Administrative reforms and the four-ruler system must be evaluated separately.
outcome_summary: The four-ruler succession arrangement did not endure after Diocletian’s retirement, while parts of the wider administrative transformation lasted much longer. The failure of one succession mechanism did not erase every other reform.

sections.title: What happened
sections.html:
Mixed outcomes. The four-ruler succession arrangement did not endure after Diocletian’s retirement, while parts of the wider administrative transformation lasted much longer. The failure of one succession mechanism did not erase every other reform.

  • The arrangement named two senior emperors, the Augusti, and two subordinate emperors, the Caesars. The Roman Empire (27 B.C.–393 A.D.)
  • The tetrarchy was short-lived, while broader changes in government helped shape the later empire. The Empire of the Tetrarchs: Imperial Pronouncements and Government

sections.title: What might explain it
sections.html:
Plausible

A succession system dependent on the founder’s arbitration was vulnerable when that arbitration disappeared. Great Founder Theory — 2020 manuscript The Empire of the Tetrarchs: Imperial Pronouncements and Government

Alternative explanation: Rival dynastic claims and control of military resources may explain instability better than complexity alone.

Plausible

Giving juniors current authority created useful experience but also an independent power base. Great Founder Theory — 2020 manuscript

Alternative explanation: Regional administrative demands may have required distributed authority regardless of succession concerns.

sections.title: Understanding the outcome
sections.html:
Founder dependence and power succession

A founder may resolve disputes that the formal succession rules leave open. Retirement tests whether successors can obtain cooperation through the rules without that person’s intervention. Great Founder Theory — 2020 manuscript The Empire of the Tetrarchs: Imperial Pronouncements and Government

The emperors controlled military and territorial resources. Ordinary deputy roles do not carry the same independent capacity to contest a succession.

sections.title: Questions to take into practice
sections.html:
• Can successors use the rules to resolve a dispute without the founder?
  • Which parts of a reform survived even when its most visible arrangement collapsed?

sections.title: What remains uncertain
sections.html: • Did the succession order fail mainly because the founder could no longer arbitrate, because rivals commanded military support, or because dynastic claims overrode the intended rules? The sequence of alliances and disputes matters for separating these explanations.

title: Botswana: continuity also survives an opposition victory
question: Can political continuity survive replacement of the governing party?
summary: Botswana’s long period of government by the Botswana Democratic Party ended with a peaceful handover to the opposition in 2024. President Mokgweetsi Masisi conceded defeat, and Duma Boko took office. The transition showed that orderly succession could extend beyond the ruling party’s own choice of leaders.
outcome_summary: The 2024 handover preserved continuity while replacing the governing party. Election observers assessed the process as peaceful and credible, while identifying weaknesses in electoral inclusion and administration. Orderly transfer and equal access to political participation remain separate achievements.

sections.title: What happened
sections.html:
Mixed outcomes. The 2024 handover preserved continuity while replacing the governing party. Election observers assessed the process as peaceful and credible, while identifying weaknesses in electoral inclusion and administration. Orderly transfer and equal access to political participation remain separate achievements.

  • Masisi conceded the 2024 election and a formal handover brought Boko into office. Botswana Presidential and National Assembly Elections: 30 October 2024
  • Election observers assessed the process as peaceful and credible, while identifying areas where inclusion and administration needed improvement. Botswana Presidential and National Assembly Elections: 30 October 2024

sections.title: What might explain it
sections.html:
Plausible

Prepared successors and elite cooperation contributed to continuity before alternation. Great Founder Theory — 2020 manuscript An African Success Story: Botswana

Alternative explanation: Electoral legitimacy, material interests and public institutions could sustain continuity independently of a single family.

Supported in case

Acceptance of electoral defeat indicates that meaningful succession rules extended beyond the governing party. Botswana Presidential and National Assembly Elections: 30 October 2024

Alternative explanation: The particular margin of defeat and choices of the leaders involved may have mattered alongside established succession rules.

sections.title: Understanding the outcome
sections.html:
Institutions, elite incentives and leadership

Continuity within one party can depend on its internal relationships. A transfer to the opposition tests whether cooperation survives when those relationships no longer determine who holds office. An African Success Story: Botswana Botswana Presidential and National Assembly Elections: 30 October 2024

A peaceful handover reveals something about succession, but does not by itself explain economic growth or show that political participation is equally accessible to everyone.

sections.title: Questions to take into practice
sections.html:
• What event would make the current explanation less convincing?
  • Can continuity survive replacement by people outside the incumbent’s chosen circle?

sections.title: What remains uncertain
sections.html: • What enabled incumbents and their supporters to accept defeat? The handover cannot by itself disentangle the roles of electoral institutions, elite cooperation, and economic interests, or explain Botswana’s longer-run economic development.

title: Japanese adopted heirs: succession beyond the bloodline
question: Does keeping family control require choosing a biological heir?
summary: Japanese business families can bring adults into the family through adoption or marriage, widening succession beyond biological children while retaining family control. Comparisons of listed firms suggest that these non-blood heirs can perform differently from biological heirs. The distinction matters: family succession is not one uniform way of selecting a leader.
outcome_summary: In the Japanese firm study, non-blood heirs performed better than blood heirs on the measures examined. Research on Danish firms found poorer performance following family CEO succession. The populations and succession arrangements differ, so the findings raise questions about how candidates are selected rather than settling whether family control is generally better.

sections.title: What happened
sections.html:
Mixed outcomes. In the Japanese firm study, non-blood heirs performed better than blood heirs on the measures examined. Research on Danish firms found poorer performance following family CEO succession. The populations and succession arrangements differ, so the findings raise questions about how candidates are selected rather than settling whether family control is generally better.

  • A study of Japanese listed firms grouped adopted sons, sons-in-law, and adopted sons-in-law as non-blood heirs and found favorable performance comparisons with blood heirs. Adoptive Expectations: Rising Sons in Japanese Family Firms
  • In a Danish study, family CEO succession was associated with poorer performance in an analysis using firstborn-child gender to help distinguish succession choices from other firm differences. Inside the Family Firm: The Role of Families in Succession Decisions and Performance

sections.title: What might explain it
sections.html:
Plausible

Allowing an outsider to become a family successor can widen the candidate pool while preserving continuity. Adoptive Expectations: Rising Sons in Japanese Family Firms

Alternative explanation: Firms able to attract strong candidates may already differ in ways that drive performance.

Plausible

The threat of replacement may change effort by biological heirs and professional managers. Adoptive Expectations: Rising Sons in Japanese Family Firms

Alternative explanation: Succession results do not separately identify selection from these proposed incentive effects.

sections.title: Understanding the outcome
sections.html:
Succession, selection and agency

A succession rule changes who can become a candidate and what incentives existing candidates face. Bringing an outsider into the family can widen selection while preserving relationships associated with family control. Adoptive Expectations: Rising Sons in Japanese Family Firms Inside the Family Firm: The Role of Families in Succession Decisions and Performance

Adoption and marriage carry legal, cultural, and personal commitments. A favorable business-performance comparison does not tell us how the people entering those relationships experienced them.

sections.title: Questions to take into practice
sections.html:
• Can the successor pool widen without losing necessary trust and knowledge?
  • What evidence distinguishes good selection from a favorable inherited business?

sections.title: What remains uncertain
sections.html: • Were stronger candidates selected, did the prospect of competing for succession change behavior, or were firms attracting non-blood heirs already different? The perspectives of spouses and candidates excluded from succession are also missing from the performance comparison.

sections.title: Sources
sections.html: • Great Founder Theory — 2020 manuscript — Samo Burja

title: Confucian transmission: preserving a tradition by changing it
question: When is adaptation a form of preservation rather than a failure to copy?
period: Late Zhou through Han and later reception
summary: Teaching, texts, ritual practice, and political sponsorship carried Confucian traditions across generations. Transmission also changed the tradition: later teachers and governments selected and interpreted texts for purposes that differed from those of earlier participants. Preserving an influential tradition was not the same as reproducing one founder’s design unchanged.
outcome_summary: Confucian traditions became influential long after Confucius’s lifetime. Their later place in curricula and government depended on interpretation and adaptation. The surviving accounts do not let us reconstruct every aspect of Confucius’s own intentions or teaching with equal confidence.

sections.title: What happened
sections.html:
Mixed outcomes. Confucian traditions became influential long after Confucius’s lifetime. Their later place in curricula and government depended on interpretation and adaptation. The surviving accounts do not let us reconstruct every aspect of Confucius’s own intentions or teaching with equal confidence.

  • Sources for Confucius’s life postdate his lifetime and differ in character and purpose. Confucius (551–479 BCE)
  • By the Han, texts associated with Confucius had become authoritative in several domains and connected with government teaching positions. Confucius
  • Later Neo-Confucian interpretation placed the Analects within a different curricular and conceptual arrangement. Confucius

sections.title: What might explain it
sections.html:
Plausible

Teaching lineages and reusable texts enabled ideas to survive a founder’s limited immediate influence. Confucius Great Founder Theory — 2020 manuscript

Alternative explanation: State adoption and reinterpretation by later thinkers may have been more decisive than fidelity to the founder.

Plausible

Ritual practice can preserve coordination knowledge that a written rule alone misses. Great Founder Theory — 2020 manuscript Confucius (551–479 BCE)

Alternative explanation: Ritual can also preserve rank and convention without preserving the function attributed to it.

sections.title: Understanding the outcome
sections.html:
Cultural transmission and institutional reconstruction

A text can survive while its interpretation changes; a ritual can continue while the relationships around it are transformed. Transmission therefore involves people who teach, interpret, and authorize practice, as well as preserved documents. Confucius Confucius (551–479 BCE) Great Founder Theory — 2020 manuscript

The persistence of a tradition does not show that every surviving practice still performs its earlier function, or that it originated with a single founder.

sections.title: Questions to take into practice
sections.html:
• Which parts of a tradition are practiced, and which only quoted?
  • What adaptations made transmission possible, and who authorized them?

sections.title: What remains uncertain
sections.html: • Which practices continued from earlier communities, and which were later reconstructions given ancient authority? Texts written after Confucius’s lifetime make it difficult to separate his intentions from the meanings later readers attached to him.

title: Latter-day Saint missions: recruitment is not retention
question: How does a repeatable recruitment system connect to durable belonging?
summary: Missionary preparation combines a shared curriculum, practice teaching, standards, and language learning. Successive cohorts can learn a recognizable way to conduct outreach. But bringing someone into a religious community is only a beginning: continued participation also depends on local relationships and the experience of membership.
outcome_summary: A repeatable training and outreach system operates across successive missionary cohorts. Conversion and retention vary across settings, and recruitment totals alone do not show how many people develop lasting participation.

sections.title: What happened
sections.html:
Mixed outcomes. A repeatable training and outreach system operates across successive missionary cohorts. Conversion and retention vary across settings, and recruitment totals alone do not show how many people develop lasting participation.

  • Missionary training includes study, practice teaching, preparation for missionary life, and initial language learning. Missionary Training Centers
  • Centralized administrative changes beginning in the 1960s altered the organization of church activity; conversion and retention varied geographically during later decades. Conversion and Retention in Mormonism

sections.title: What might explain it
sections.html:
Plausible

Shared training and curriculum can make outreach repeatable across cohorts. Missionary Training Centers

Alternative explanation: Participants are self-selected and supported by a wider religious community; training is only one component.

Plausible

Standardized recruitment may fit local community integration unevenly. Conversion and Retention in Mormonism

Alternative explanation: Migration, existing relationships, economic circumstances and different meanings of membership may also explain retention.

sections.title: Understanding the outcome
sections.html:
Organizational socialization and conversion careers

Training can make an invitation repeatable, while durable belonging depends on what happens after that invitation is accepted. Local relationships connect the recruitment process to continuing participation. Missionary Training Centers Conversion and Retention in Mormonism

Religious commitment involves beliefs, family relationships, and personal meaning. Recruitment practices detached from that setting may work differently.

sections.title: Questions to take into practice
sections.html:
• What happens six months after someone joins?
  • Does onboarding develop local relationships as well as transmit a standard message?

sections.title: What remains uncertain
sections.html: • How do local relationships, migration, material circumstances, and administrative practices affect participation after conversion? Following people who remain, leave, or participate intermittently would reveal more than a single membership total.

sections.title: Sources
sections.html: • Great Founder Theory — 2020 manuscript — Samo Burja

title: Protestant literacy: competing explanations for prosperity
question: Can an ideology create useful capabilities without its official purpose being economic?
period: Historical German lands; nineteenth-century Prussian comparison
summary: Religious expectations about reading could encourage skills useful outside religious life. Historical research on Prussian counties found evidence consistent with literacy explaining much of the prosperity difference associated with Protestantism. A separate study of long-run city growth found no Protestant growth advantage, raising a question about which economic outcomes the proposed mechanism can explain.
outcome_summary: Prussian county results are consistent with literacy explaining much of an observed prosperity gap. A separate city-growth study finds no Protestant growth advantage over its long period. Different units and outcomes prevent treating either finding as a universal verdict on religion and prosperity.

sections.title: What happened
sections.html:
Mixed outcomes. Prussian county results are consistent with literacy explaining much of an observed prosperity gap. A separate city-growth study finds no Protestant growth advantage over its long period. Different units and outcomes prevent treating either finding as a universal verdict on religion and prosperity.

  • Becker and Woessmann use county data and distance to Wittenberg as an instrument for Protestantism. Was Weber Wrong? A Human Capital Theory of Protestant Economic History
  • They report results consistent with literacy accounting for much of the economic difference. Was Weber Wrong? A Human Capital Theory of Protestant Economic History
  • Cantoni studies population in 272 cities from 1300–1900 and reports no growth effect of Protestantism. The Economic Effects of the Protestant Reformation: Testing the Weber Hypothesis in the German Lands

sections.title: What might explain it
sections.html:
Supported in case

Religious reading expectations generated skills useful outside religious practice. Was Weber Wrong? A Human Capital Theory of Protestant Economic History

Alternative explanation: The interpretation depends on instrument validity and the separation of religion from other geographically patterned influences.

Plausible

Different outcome measures and time scales explain part of the apparent disagreement. Was Weber Wrong? A Human Capital Theory of Protestant Economic History The Economic Effects of the Protestant Reformation: Testing the Weber Hypothesis in the German Lands

Alternative explanation: Further comparison might reveal genuinely incompatible results rather than merely different measurements.

sections.title: Understanding the outcome
sections.html:
Human capital versus cultural work-ethic explanations

A religious norm might affect economic life through a practical capability such as reading, without economic improvement being its purpose. That is a different explanation from claiming that belief directly produces a stronger work ethic. Was Weber Wrong? A Human Capital Theory of Protestant Economic History The Economic Effects of the Protestant Reformation: Testing the Weber Hypothesis in the German Lands

The studies concern particular historical populations and periods. Their results do not establish that changing religious affiliation would produce the same capabilities or outcomes elsewhere.

sections.title: Questions to take into practice
sections.html:
• Which observable skill mediates the claimed cultural effect?
  • Would the explanation survive a different measure of success or period?

sections.title: What remains uncertain
sections.html: • Could geography or other historical differences explain both religious affiliation and prosperity? The literacy explanation depends on separating those influences. It also remains important to understand why a result about county prosperity does not appear as a general advantage in long-run city growth.

sections.title: Sources
sections.html: • Great Founder Theory — 2020 manuscript — Samo Burja

title: FOGBANK: documentation is not a living capability
question: How do institutions discover that a capability they once had no longer exists?
summary: When a defense program needed to resume a discontinued production activity, the organization no longer had all the knowledge, expertise, and facilities needed to perform it. Reestablishing the capability took additional time and money. The episode shows how an organization can retain a requirement and records of earlier work while losing the practical ability to carry it out.
outcome_summary: Reestablishing the production capability delayed the program by a year and required $69 million to address the problem, according to the public audit. Missing knowledge was part of the failure, alongside weaknesses in managing a known program risk.

sections.title: What happened
sections.html:
Failure on the stated objective. Reestablishing the production capability delayed the program by a year and required $69 million to address the problem, according to the public audit. Missing knowledge was part of the failure, alongside weaknesses in managing a known program risk.

  • The public audit identified missing knowledge, expertise, and facilities, together with ineffective execution of a risk-management strategy. NNSA and DOD Need to More Effectively Manage the Stockpile Life Extension Program
  • The audit reported a one-year delay and $69 million associated with resolving the production problem. NNSA and DOD Need to More Effectively Manage the Stockpile Life Extension Program

sections.title: What might explain it
sections.html:
Supported in case

Capability disappeared when knowledge, people and supporting infrastructure were not maintained together. NNSA and DOD Need to More Effectively Manage the Stockpile Life Extension Program

Alternative explanation: Budgeting and execution failures contributed; attributing everything to unwritten knowledge would be incomplete.

Plausible

Periodic demonstrations by successors could reveal hidden capability loss earlier than document reviews. Great Founder Theory — 2020 manuscript

Alternative explanation: This proposed intervention was not evaluated in the audit and could be costly or impractical in some settings.

sections.title: Understanding the outcome
sections.html:
Organizational memory and tacit knowledge

Documentation is useful only alongside people and facilities able to turn it into action. Separately changing staff, budgets, and infrastructure can leave responsibility for the combined capability unclear. NNSA and DOD Need to More Effectively Manage the Stockpile Life Extension Program Great Founder Theory — 2020 manuscript

Specialized production can have unusually expensive restart requirements. The size of this loss cannot be used to estimate the cost of ordinary staff turnover.

sections.title: Questions to take into practice
sections.html:
• What critical activity has not been performed successfully by the next generation?
  • Who owns continuity risk when facilities, staff and budgets change separately?

sections.title: What remains uncertain
sections.html: • Which losses were most consequential: experienced personnel, practical knowledge, facilities, or failures to act on the known risk? Demonstrations by successor teams might have exposed the gap earlier, but their cost and usefulness were not tested in this episode.

sections.title: Sources
sections.html: • Additional Actions Could Help Improve Management of Activities Involving Explosive Materials — US Government Accountability Office, GAO-19-449

title: Bell Labs: discovery and diffusion need different arrangements
question: Can the institution producing breakthroughs also obstruct their wider use?
summary: Bell Labs paired sustained industrial research with a powerful incumbent business. The 1956 antitrust settlement required royalty-free licensing of existing patents. This case separates an organization’s ability to invent from the legal and competitive conditions under which others can build on those inventions.
outcome_summary: The laboratory produced important discoveries, while the patent study finds increased follow-on innovation after compulsory licensing outside telecommunications. The sectoral exception matters: access to knowledge did not remove every market barrier.

sections.title: What happened
sections.html:
Mixed outcomes. The laboratory produced important discoveries, while the patent study finds increased follow-on innovation after compulsory licensing outside telecommunications. The sectoral exception matters: access to knowledge did not remove every market barrier.

  • Bell Labs’ research capacity was connected to the telephone system and to an organization combining research with development work. History of Bell Labs
  • The 1956 decree required royalty-free licensing of existing Bell patents. How Antitrust Enforcement Can Spur Innovation: Bell Labs and the 1956 Consent Decree
  • A comparison with non-Bell patents found lasting increases in follow-on patenting outside telecommunications, but not inside the sector. How Antitrust Enforcement Can Spur Innovation: Bell Labs and the 1956 Consent Decree

sections.title: What might explain it
sections.html:
Plausible

Stable resources and links between research and engineering supported discovery. History of Bell Labs

Alternative explanation: Selection of exceptional researchers and the field’s scientific opportunities could explain much of the output.

Supported in case

Patent access alone was insufficient where other barriers continued to constrain entry. How Antitrust Enforcement Can Spur Innovation: Bell Labs and the 1956 Consent Decree

Alternative explanation: Differences in opportunities and conditions across sectors may also contribute to the contrast; licensing was not the only feature that varied.

sections.title: Understanding the outcome
sections.html:
Knowledge spillovers and barriers to entry

Permission to use an invention removes one barrier. Firms may still need customers, equipment, distribution, or access to a market dominated by an incumbent. How Antitrust Enforcement Can Spur Innovation: Bell Labs and the 1956 Consent Decree

Follow-on patenting captures only part of innovation. It does not show every useful improvement, commercial application, or benefit to the public.

sections.title: Questions to take into practice
sections.html:
• Does the research organization enable outsiders to build on its work?
  • Which barriers remain after formal access is opened?

sections.title: What remains uncertain
sections.html: • Did wider licensing change Bell’s own incentive to invest in research over the longer term? Which remaining barriers explain the different result inside telecommunications? More follow-on patents do not, by themselves, measure every benefit or cost to users.

title: Xerox PARC: invention needs a route into the world
question: Why can a productive research organization fail to capture some of what it creates?
summary: PARC developed prototypes and technical communities whose influence spread beyond Xerox. Some technologies found a route to users through spin-offs with different customers and revenue models. A productive research organization still needed a way to connect its inventions to development, distribution, and a viable business.
outcome_summary: PARC’s inventions had substantial influence, while Xerox and the spin-offs captured value unevenly. In a comparison of selected spin-offs, successful ventures changed their business models more than unsuccessful ventures. The later outcome does not reveal which opportunities were clearly promising when the decisions were made.

sections.title: What happened
sections.html:
Mixed outcomes. PARC’s inventions had substantial influence, while Xerox and the spin-offs captured value unevenly. In a comparison of selected spin-offs, successful ventures changed their business models more than unsuccessful ventures. The later outcome does not reveal which opportunities were clearly promising when the decisions were made.

  • PARC engineers developed the Alto through intensive prototyping and use within their technical community. Xerox PARC’s Engineers on How They Invented the Future
  • Among the Xerox technology spin-offs compared in the study, successful ventures changed their business models, while failed ventures showed less search and learning. The Role of the Business Model in Capturing Value from Innovation: Evidence from Xerox Corporation’s Technology Spinoff Companies

sections.title: What might explain it
sections.html:
Supported in case

A successful existing business model can narrow which new uses an organization can recognize and support. The Role of the Business Model in Capturing Value from Innovation: Evidence from Xerox Corporation’s Technology Spinoff Companies

Alternative explanation: Markets, complementary technology and timing may make apparently promising uses unviable regardless of management interpretation.

Plausible

Spin-offs can create room for a different customer and revenue model. The Role of the Business Model in Capturing Value from Innovation: Evidence from Xerox Corporation’s Technology Spinoff Companies

Alternative explanation: Spin-offs also lose resources and coordination benefits; selected survivors exaggerate their apparent advantage.

sections.title: Understanding the outcome
sections.html:
Business models as an organizational learning mechanism

A prototype can be technically impressive while lacking a customer, distribution channel, service arrangement, or source of revenue. Testing those connections is part of learning what the invention can become. The Role of the Business Model in Capturing Value from Innovation: Evidence from Xerox Corporation’s Technology Spinoff Companies

A retrospective account benefits from knowing what later succeeded. It cannot show that every rejected experiment would have been sensible to fund at the time.

sections.title: Questions to take into practice
sections.html:
• Who owns the work of turning a prototype into a usable service?
  • Can a new idea test a different business model without satisfying all assumptions of the old one?

sections.title: What remains uncertain
sections.html: • How many apparently promising spin-offs failed, and which inventions were commercialized successfully inside Xerox? Without both sides of that comparison, it is easy to mistake the most memorable successes elsewhere for a complete account of Xerox’s choices.

title: NUMMI: changing the work changed the culture
question: Can people learn a new way of organizing without replacing the workforce?
summary: Toyota and GM used the NUMMI joint venture to combine car production with organizational learning. Training and changes in daily management accompanied reported improvements among a workforce previously regarded as difficult. The plant later closed, showing why improving work and sustaining a business need to be examined separately.
outcome_summary: Participants reported improvements in quality and attendance, and research traced learning from Toyota through NUMMI to GM. The plant nevertheless closed after GM’s withdrawal and Toyota’s assessment that continued operation was not viable.

sections.title: What happened
sections.html:
Mixed outcomes. Participants reported improvements in quality and attendance, and research traced learning from Toyota through NUMMI to GM. The plant nevertheless closed after GM’s withdrawal and Toyota’s assessment that continued operation was not viable.

  • John Shook, who participated in the venture, described changes in training and management accompanied by lower absenteeism and better quality. How to Change a Culture: Lessons from NUMMI
  • Knowledge developed through the Toyota–GM partnership was transferred beyond NUMMI into GM. Learning Through Alliances: General Motors and NUMMI
  • Toyota announced the end of production after GM’s withdrawal, citing economic viability. TMC to End Production Contract with NUMMI in March 2010

sections.title: What might explain it
sections.html:
Participant explanation

Changing routines and how problems receive help can change the experience that sustains workplace norms. How to Change a Culture: Lessons from NUMMI

Alternative explanation: Restart conditions, selection and economic circumstances may contribute to the reported improvement.

Plausible

Learning transfers through relationships and participation, not simply copying visible artifacts. Learning Through Alliances: General Motors and NUMMI

Alternative explanation: Training, management decisions, and formal documentation may have worked together with relationships; their separate contributions are difficult to isolate.

sections.title: Understanding the outcome
sections.html:
Organizational learning and knowledge transfer

People learn an unfamiliar work system through what happens when they identify a problem, ask for help, or attempt a task. The daily response can change expectations more than a statement about organizational culture. How to Change a Culture: Lessons from NUMMI Learning Through Alliances: General Motors and NUMMI

The joint venture had access to Toyota’s training and GM’s organization. Another workplace would need to establish who can teach the practice and support it after training ends.

sections.title: Questions to take into practice
sections.html:
• What changes in the daily handling of a problem?
  • Can another part of the organization reproduce the practice with its own people?

sections.title: What remains uncertain
sections.html: • How did workers experience the changes, and how much of the reported improvement came from the work system rather than restart conditions or selection? GM’s withdrawal and Toyota’s commercial judgment also leave questions about how benefits and costs were distributed between the partners.

title: Surgical checklists: a form is not an implementation
question: Why can a promising practice produce different results at scale?
summary: A surgical checklist organizes pauses, shared confirmation, and critical tasks. An early eight-hospital study found improved outcomes after its introduction; a later Ontario study did not find significant improvements after broad adoption. The contrast raises a concrete question: what must change in daily teamwork for a checklist to affect care?
outcome_summary: The pilot reported lower mortality and complications. Ontario’s 101-hospital comparison found no statistically significant reduction. Both were before-and-after studies, so differences cannot automatically be attributed to implementation quality or the checklist itself.

sections.title: What happened
sections.html:
Mixed outcomes. The pilot reported lower mortality and complications. Ontario’s 101-hospital comparison found no statistically significant reduction. Both were before-and-after studies, so differences cannot automatically be attributed to implementation quality or the checklist itself.

  • The eight-hospital study compared 3,733 patients before and 3,955 after introduction and reported reductions in death and complications. A Surgical Safety Checklist to Reduce Morbidity and Mortality in a Global Population
  • The Ontario study analyzed more than 200,000 procedures across 101 hospitals and found no significant mortality or complication improvement. Introduction of Surgical Safety Checklists in Ontario, Canada
  • An earlier systematic review reported favorable pooled results but variable compliance and a need for implementation research. It predates Ontario. A Systematic Review of the Effectiveness, Compliance, and Critical Factors for Implementation of Safety Checklists in Surgery

sections.title: What might explain it
sections.html:
Plausible

Actual team use and integration into work may matter more than formally adopting a checklist. A Systematic Review of the Effectiveness, Compliance, and Critical Factors for Implementation of Safety Checklists in Surgery

Alternative explanation: Different baseline risks, outcomes and observation methods could also explain the contrast.

Plausible

Before-and-after improvements may partly reflect concurrent changes or observation effects. A Surgical Safety Checklist to Reduce Morbidity and Mortality in a Global Population Introduction of Surgical Safety Checklists in Ontario, Canada

Alternative explanation: A real benefit could still exist; absence of randomization limits attribution rather than disproving effectiveness.

sections.title: Understanding the outcome
sections.html:
Implementation fidelity and context

Official adoption does not show whether staff paused, checked the relevant information, and acted on a problem. Those behaviors connect the checklist to the outcome it is intended to improve. A Surgical Safety Checklist to Reduce Morbidity and Mortality in a Global Population Introduction of Surgical Safety Checklists in Ontario, Canada A Systematic Review of the Effectiveness, Compliance, and Critical Factors for Implementation of Safety Checklists in Surgery

A checklist’s value depends on the work, baseline practice, and response to an identified problem. Results from surgery cannot supply an effect size for a checklist in a different setting.

sections.title: Questions to take into practice
sections.html:
• Was the practice performed meaningfully or merely recorded as completed?
  • What baseline and comparison would show improvement rather than a change in reporting?

sections.title: What remains uncertain
sections.html: • Were teams using the checklist differently, or did the hospitals start from different levels of risk and safety practice? Changes in patient mix, concurrent improvements, and measurement could also affect the comparison. The before-and-after designs cannot cleanly separate those explanations.

title: Athens: citizens governing, but not everyone was a citizen
question: How did assembly participation, lottery, elected expertise, and scrutiny work together—and whom did they exclude?
period: 508–322 BCE; institutional description mainly fourth century BCE
summary: Classical Athens combined citizen assemblies, a council selected by lot, elected offices, and large popular juries. In the fourth century BCE, eligible male citizens could participate directly without becoming professional politicians. Most inhabitants were excluded from citizenship, however, and even among citizens only a fraction attended any particular assembly.
outcome_summary: The institutions enabled substantial direct participation among eligible male citizens and distributed many offices beyond professional politicians. That achievement coexisted with slavery, exclusions based on gender and citizenship, uneven attendance, and oligarchic interruptions. Broad participation within the citizen body did not mean political equality for the whole population or agreement about the quality of decisions.

sections.title: What happened
sections.html:
Mixed outcomes. The institutions enabled substantial direct participation among eligible male citizens and distributed many offices beyond professional politicians. That achievement coexisted with slavery, exclusions based on gender and citizenship, uneven attendance, and oligarchic interruptions. Broad participation within the citizen body did not mean political equality for the whole population or agreement about the quality of decisions.

  • Adult male citizenship, rather than residence alone, determined assembly eligibility; enrollment included checks of age, freedom, and parentage. Athenian Democracy: A Brief Overview
  • The council and many offices used allotment, while some responsibilities used election; incoming magistrates underwent scrutiny rather than receiving unchecked authority. The Athenian Constitution, parts 43–69 Athenian Democracy: A Brief Overview
  • The eligible citizen body is estimated at around 30,000 in the fourth century, with meetings attended by thousands rather than everyone. Assembly pay helped make attendance possible, although urban residents remained better placed to attend. Democratic deliberation in the Athenian Assembly: procedures and behaviours towards legitimacy

sections.title: What might explain it
sections.html:
Plausible

Rotating opportunities to govern, combined with scrutiny, plausibly reduced the permanence of an officeholding class among eligible citizens. The Athenian Constitution, parts 43–69 Athenian Democracy: A Brief Overview

Alternative explanation: Wealth, rhetorical skill, military prominence, and repeated informal leadership could sustain elite influence without permanent formal office.

Supported in case

Payment plausibly made attendance less costly for citizens who would otherwise give up earnings to participate. Democratic deliberation in the Athenian Assembly: procedures and behaviours towards legitimacy

Alternative explanation: Proximity to the meeting place and the political salience of particular decisions also affected who appeared.

sections.title: Understanding the outcome
sections.html:
Deliberation and political participation in classical Athenian assemblies

Participation depended on an interacting institutional package, not only a voting rule. Democratic deliberation in the Athenian Assembly: procedures and behaviours towards legitimacy

Eligibility, travel distances, and the resources supporting participation differed sharply from those in a modern electorate. The institutions also changed across Athens's democratic periods.

sections.title: Questions to take into practice
sections.html:
• A right to attend and a practical opportunity to attend are different: citizenship rules, payment, and distance all shaped who was in the assembly.
  • Lottery and rotation spread offices, while scrutiny and elected roles added other forms of accountability and expertise.

sections.title: What remains uncertain
sections.html:
• Estimates of meeting attendance vary, making it difficult to establish how consistently different parts of the citizen body participated.
  • Lottery, payment, and scrutiny operated together within an economy and imperial position unlike those of most modern communities; their separate contributions remain difficult to establish.

title: Porto Alegre: a budget people could shape—and a process politicians could hollow out
question: What makes participation consequential, and what allows it to lose that force?
period: 1989–2017, with earlier gains and later decline distinguished
summary: Porto Alegre linked neighborhood participation to municipal investment priorities through recurring assemblies and budgeting arrangements. Residents could press for infrastructure that had bypassed poorer areas. Early gains were followed by weakened political backing, implementation problems, and suspension in 2017: residents' ability to influence investment depended on more than having meetings.
outcome_summary: The early process mobilized poorer communities and helped improve access to smaller-scale infrastructure. Water, sanitation, and other services were also changing through a broader municipal policy program, so the gains cannot be assigned to participatory budgeting alone. As political support and implementation weakened, participation lost influence over investment; the process was suspended in 2017.

sections.title: What happened
sections.html:
Mixed outcomes. The early process mobilized poorer communities and helped improve access to smaller-scale infrastructure. Water, sanitation, and other services were also changing through a broader municipal policy program, so the gains cannot be assigned to participatory budgeting alone. As political support and implementation weakened, participation lost influence over investment; the process was suspended in 2017.

  • The city tied participatory priorities to investment decisions and used the process to involve communities previously poorly served by infrastructure. Porto Alegre: Participatory Budgeting and the Challenge of Sustaining Transformative Change
  • By 2002, extensive water, sanitation, waste, environmental-information, and education policies were operating alongside participatory budgeting. Participatory democracy and sustainable development: integrated urban environmental management in Porto Alegre, Brazil
  • Political support declined and the process was suspended in 2017, following weakened financial and implementation commitments. Porto Alegre: Participatory Budgeting and the Challenge of Sustaining Transformative Change

sections.title: What might explain it
sections.html:
Supported in case

Participation became consequential when priority-setting connected to a funded and responsive municipal implementation system. Porto Alegre: Participatory Budgeting and the Challenge of Sustaining Transformative Change Participatory democracy and sustainable development: integrated urban environmental management in Porto Alegre, Brazil

Alternative explanation: The governing party's redistributive agenda and capable service agencies could have driven some improvements independently of citizen meetings.

Supported in case

The later weakening suggests that participation depended on renewed political backing and funding, not simply on keeping its formal procedures. Porto Alegre: Participatory Budgeting and the Challenge of Sustaining Transformative Change

Alternative explanation: Wider fiscal constraints could have reduced investment even under a government strongly committed to the participatory process.

sections.title: Understanding the outcome
sections.html:
Participatory governance embedded in state capacity

Public voice connects to distribution through budgeting, administration, and political support. Porto Alegre: Participatory Budgeting and the Challenge of Sustaining Transformative Change Participatory democracy and sustainable development: integrated urban environmental management in Porto Alegre, Brazil

Organized civil society, service agencies, and political commitments gave the assemblies ways to influence spending. An assembly without those connections would lack much of that capacity.

sections.title: Questions to take into practice
sections.html:
• Participation changes investment only when the priorities residents set reach funded projects and responsible implementing agencies.
  • Attendance can remain visible while completion stalls; project delivery and whose needs are served reveal a different part of the result.
  • A change in governing coalition can weaken the commitments that made a participatory process consequential.

sections.title: What remains uncertain
sections.html:
• The early improvements were intertwined with wider municipal reforms, leaving uncertainty about how much each contributed.
  • The decline raises a durability question: which commitments can protect residents' influence when budgets tighten or a governing coalition changes?

title: Ireland: a citizens' assembly inside a larger route to constitutional change
question: How can a small deliberating group inform a decision that remains with the wider electorate?
summary: Ireland's assembly brought 99 selected citizens together under an appointed chair to consider several issues, beginning with the Eighth Amendment. Evidence, deliberation, and recommendations fed into parliamentary consideration and a national referendum. The assembly helped develop proposals; it neither represented every resident nor possessed the authority to amend the constitution by itself.
outcome_summary: The assembly produced recommendations that entered parliamentary consideration and were followed by a constitutional referendum in 2018. The electorate approved the amendment. Assembly discussion showed substantial cognitive complexity in the exchanges examined, but the referendum result also emerged from a wider political campaign and changing public attitudes.

sections.title: What happened
sections.html:
Bounded success. The assembly produced recommendations that entered parliamentary consideration and were followed by a constitutional referendum in 2018. The electorate approved the amendment. Assembly discussion showed substantial cognitive complexity in the exchanges examined, but the referendum result also emerged from a wider political campaign and changing public attitudes.

  • The parliamentary mandate specified an appointed chair and 99 referendum-eligible citizens selected to broadly reflect Irish society. First Report and Recommendations: The Eighth Amendment of the Constitution
  • A comparative analysis of assembly and parliamentary committee debate found deeper cognitive complexity among assembly members in the discussions studied. Measuring Epistemic Deliberation on Polarized Issues: The Case of Abortion Provision in Ireland
  • The referendum recorded 1,429,981 votes for the constitutional proposal and 723,632 against, with turnout of 64.13%. Referendum on the Thirty-sixth Amendment of the Constitution Bill 2018

sections.title: What might explain it
sections.html:
Supported in case

Structured exposure to evidence in a less strategically adversarial setting contributed to nuanced discussion. Measuring Epistemic Deliberation on Polarized Issues: The Case of Abortion Provision in Ireland

Alternative explanation: Participant selection, different tasks, and the contrasting public roles of legislators could explain part of the measured difference.

Plausible

A defined path through parliament and referendum made the recommendations politically actionable. First Report and Recommendations: The Eighth Amendment of the Constitution Referendum on the Thirty-sixth Amendment of the Constitution Bill 2018

Alternative explanation: Long-running campaigning and changing public attitudes might have produced reform through another institutional route.

sections.title: Understanding the outcome
sections.html:
Epistemic deliberation and cognitive complexity

Reasoning quality can be assessed through how people recognize different considerations and connect them, separately from whether they change their preference or reach agreement. Measuring Epistemic Deliberation on Polarized Issues: The Case of Abortion Provision in Ireland

Nuanced discussion among selected participants does not show how the wider public formed its views or whose experiences the panel missed.

sections.title: Questions to take into practice
sections.html:
• The assembly could develop recommendations, while parliament and the electorate retained consequential decisions; these different roles gave the recommendations a route to action without making the panel sovereign.
  • The quality of the discussion is a separate question from whether an observer favors the resulting constitutional change.
  • A small deliberating body still needs its reasoning exposed to wider public disagreement.

sections.title: What remains uncertain
sections.html:
• How much the assembly changed referendum voters' views, compared with campaigning and longer-term attitude changes, remains uncertain.
  • Referendum eligibility excluded some residents affected by abortion policy; recruitment, attrition, and agenda choices also shaped whose experience entered the discussion.

title: Iceland: crowdsourcing a constitution without securing adoption
question: What is the difference between contributing to a draft and controlling its adoption?
summary: Following Iceland's financial crisis, a multistage constitutional process invited public input and produced a proposed constitution. Online discussion accompanied a council's drafting work rather than replacing it with an unfiltered public document. A 2012 advisory referendum supported using the proposal as a basis, but the process did not deliver an enacted replacement constitution.
outcome_summary: The process generated a substantive draft and online exchanges in which participants responded to one another, yet did not secure adoption. Participation was self-selected and uneven. Producing a draft through public contributions did not give those contributors control over the parliamentary decisions needed to turn it into a constitution.

sections.title: What happened
sections.html:
Mixed outcomes. The process generated a substantive draft and online exchanges in which participants responded to one another, yet did not secure adoption. Participation was self-selected and uneven. Producing a draft through public contributions did not give those contributors control over the parliamentary decisions needed to turn it into a constitution.

  • The public platform used moderated, non-anonymous threads with topic-setting submissions and engagement from council members. Judging Deliberation: An Assessment of the Crowdsourced Icelandic Constitutional Project
  • The three longest online discussion threads contained responsive exchanges, but participation was concentrated among a self-selected group whose demographic composition was uncertain. Judging Deliberation: An Assessment of the Crowdsourced Icelandic Constitutional Project
  • An advisory referendum supported using the draft as a basis for a new constitution, but no final parliamentary adoption vote followed in the process's 2010–2013 period. Why Do Politicians Not Act Upon Citizens' Deliberations? Evidence From Iceland

sections.title: What might explain it
sections.html:
Plausible

Clear topics, moderation, and visible links to drafters plausibly encouraged substantive exchanges. Judging Deliberation: An Assessment of the Crowdsourced Icelandic Constitutional Project

Alternative explanation: Highly interested, educated participants may have generated these qualities even without the platform's specific design.

Plausible

Participation without an enforceable or politically secured adoption pathway can produce influential text without institutional change. Why Do Politicians Not Act Upon Citizens' Deliberations? Evidence From Iceland

Alternative explanation: Disagreement over provisions and legal process, rather than a general hostility to participation, could also explain resistance.

sections.title: Understanding the outcome
sections.html:
Deliberative quality versus decisiveness in participatory constitution-making

A discussion may be deliberative without being representative, decisive, or just. Judging Deliberation: An Assessment of the Crowdsourced Icelandic Constitutional Project

The three longest online threads reveal what sustained discussion could look like, but not what less active participants experienced or whether the public as a whole was represented.

sections.title: Questions to take into practice
sections.html:
• Public input can influence a draft without giving contributors authority over its adoption.
  • An advisory referendum can endorse a direction while leaving later parliamentary decisions unresolved.
  • A high comment count can coexist with influence concentrated among relatively few contributors.

sections.title: What remains uncertain
sections.html:
• The most sustained threads may have differed from shorter exchanges and from the experience of people who did not participate.
  • The relative contributions of substantive disagreement, legal-process objections, and political resistance to the adoption failure remain difficult to separate.

title: Oregon: citizens writing a guide for other voters
question: Can a deliberating panel improve public knowledge without deciding for the electorate?
period: 2010–2018 evaluated panels; commission hiatus continuing in the 2026 official record
location: Oregon, United States, with comparison trials elsewhere
summary: Citizens' Initiative Review convened a stratified sample of voters to question advocates and experts about ballot measures, deliberate, and write a short public statement. The panel informed voters rather than replacing the referendum. Oregon placed statements in its official voters' pamphlet, but the commission later went on hiatus despite evidence that reading the statements improved policy knowledge.
