outcome_summary: Across survey experiments covering reviews in Oregon and elsewhere, readers of panel statements gained policy knowledge. That result concerns understanding after exposure to the statement, not whether every voter read it or whether the resulting policies were better. Oregon's commission had been on hiatus since 2018 as of the 2026 official record, separating the information product's value from the institution's ability to keep operating.

sections.title: What happened
sections.html:
Mixed outcomes. Across survey experiments covering reviews in Oregon and elsewhere, readers of panel statements gained policy knowledge. That result concerns understanding after exposure to the statement, not whether every voter read it or whether the resulting policies were better. Oregon's commission had been on hiatus since 2018 as of the 2026 official record, separating the information product's value from the institution's ability to keep operating.

  • Panels considered evidence and competing arguments over four to five days, then produced factual findings and pro/con arguments for voters. Deliberative panels as a source of public knowledge: A large-sample test of the Citizens' Initiative Review
  • Experiments spanning thirteen reviews and 10,872 registered voters found a positive effect of reading the statements on policy knowledge. Deliberative panels as a source of public knowledge: A large-sample test of the Citizens' Initiative Review
  • As of 2026, the commission had been on hiatus since 2018, although the official voters' pamphlet procedures still provided for its statements. State Voters' Pamphlet Manual: ELECT 1-2026

sections.title: What might explain it
sections.html:
Supported in case

A short synthesis vetted by peers can reduce the effort needed to learn about a ballot measure. Deliberative panels as a source of public knowledge: A large-sample test of the Citizens' Initiative Review

Alternative explanation: Part of the improvement may arise from receiving any concise relevant information, rather than deliberation or peer authorship specifically.

Plausible

Formal authorization is insufficient for durability if an institution lacks the resources or support to keep operating. State Voters' Pamphlet Manual: ELECT 1-2026

Alternative explanation: Inactivity could also reflect administrative or strategic choices; the existence of a hiatus does not identify which organizational commitment failed.

sections.title: Understanding the outcome
sections.html:
Deliberative mini-publics as trusted information intermediaries

The panel's output connects a small deliberative process to a much larger electorate. Deliberative panels as a source of public knowledge: A large-sample test of the Citizens' Initiative Review

Exposing research participants to a statement differs from ensuring that voters encounter and trust it in a real campaign.

sections.title: Questions to take into practice
sections.html:
• A panel can help other voters understand an issue while leaving the final vote with the electorate.
  • Publication and readership are separate: a useful statement must also reach people amid competing campaign information.
  • Legal authorization can remain in place while the organization needed to deliver the process stops operating.

sections.title: What remains uncertain
sections.html:
• The pooled knowledge result combines Oregon with other jurisdictions; effects specific to Oregon may differ.
  • The causes of the commission's hiatus remain unresolved, including the relative roles of funding, organizational capacity, and political support.

title: Nepal irrigation: better hardware was not enough
question: Why could farmer-managed systems outperform more technically sophisticated agency-managed systems?
summary: In Nepal, farmer-managed irrigation systems often operated with simpler physical works than agency-managed systems while devising and enforcing their own rules. Yet they could perform better. Water delivery depended not only on engineering but on who maintained the works, how water was allocated, and whether users could make one another keep their commitments.
outcome_summary: In the systems examined, farmer-managed irrigation had higher average performance and stronger local rule enforcement than agency-managed irrigation. The comparison points to the importance of organization alongside infrastructure. Differences in water availability, geography, and system size make it difficult to attribute the whole advantage to local management.

sections.title: What happened
sections.html:
Mixed outcomes. In the systems examined, farmer-managed irrigation had higher average performance and stronger local rule enforcement than agency-managed irrigation. The comparison points to the importance of organization alongside infrastructure. Differences in water availability, geography, and system size make it difficult to attribute the whole advantage to local management.

  • Farmer-managed systems tended to outperform state-operated systems despite comparatively low-tech infrastructure. The Performance of Self-Governing Irrigation Systems in Nepal
  • Enforcement was stronger in the farmer-managed systems with locally devised rules than in the agency-managed systems with rules made by outside officials. Rules and collective action: an institutional analysis of the performance of irrigation systems in Nepal
  • The rules operated in communities with different beliefs and biophysical conditions; management type alone did not describe all the conditions affecting cooperation. Rules and collective action: an institutional analysis of the performance of irrigation systems in Nepal

sections.title: What might explain it
sections.html:
Supported in case

Locally workable rules and credible enforcement helped sustain contributions and coordination. Rules and collective action: an institutional analysis of the performance of irrigation systems in Nepal

Alternative explanation: Water availability, system size, geography, and selection into management type could explain part of the performance difference.

Plausible

Infrastructure projects can disappoint when they alter physical works without preserving users' incentives to maintain and allocate water. The Performance of Self-Governing Irrigation Systems in Nepal Rules and collective action: an institutional analysis of the performance of irrigation systems in Nepal

Alternative explanation: Insufficient funding, staff, or maintenance quality within agencies may matter more than external rulemaking itself.

sections.title: Understanding the outcome
sections.html:
Institutional Analysis and Development; institutional grammar applied to irrigation rules

Rules in use shape users' incentives to contribute maintenance, respect allocations, and respond to violations. The Performance of Self-Governing Irrigation Systems in Nepal Rules and collective action: an institutional analysis of the performance of irrigation systems in Nepal

Local management still needs to handle water flows, infrastructure, and disputes beyond an individual community. Strong local organization and public technical support can serve different parts of the same system.

sections.title: Questions to take into practice
sections.html:
• Upgrading physical works can leave water delivery unreliable if maintenance and allocation responsibilities no longer fit users' incentives.
  • Rules written by an agency and rules people actually enforce can describe different operating systems.
  • Average performance can conceal different outcomes for users near the water source and those at the tail end.

sections.title: What remains uncertain
sections.html:
• The systems were not randomly assigned to management arrangements, so geography, water supply, and prior community organization may explain some of the observed difference.
  • The distribution of gains between head-end and tail-end users remains important even where average system performance is higher.

title: Törbel: a commons with boundaries, private property, and exclusions
question: How can collective ownership work together with private holdings—and reproduce inequalities?
period: Historical commoner institutions described in twentieth-century research
summary: Törbel's alpine economy combined private household land with collectively managed pasture, forest, and irrigation resources. Rules linked summer grazing to the animals households could support in winter and organized maintenance obligations. This was neither open access nor an entirely communal economy: belonging, property, and participation rights determined who could benefit and influence decisions.
outcome_summary: Collective management of alpine resources endured alongside private household holdings. Grazing access and maintenance obligations linked households to the commons, while membership boundaries excluded outsiders. Durability therefore coexisted with unequal rights; the arrangement was not open access or an equal claim for every resident.

sections.title: What happened
sections.html:
Mixed outcomes. Collective management of alpine resources endured alongside private household holdings. Grazing access and maintenance obligations linked households to the commons, while membership boundaries excluded outsiders. Durability therefore coexisted with unequal rights; the arrangement was not open access or an equal claim for every resident.

  • Privately held fields coexisted with common alpine resources; grazing access was constrained by households' winter-support capacity and linked to maintenance responsibilities. Governing the Commons: The Evolution of Institutions for Collective Action
  • Household property, collective work, and membership rights operated together rather than forming separate private and communal economies. Swiss commoners' struggles for the right balance: Ontologies, identities and responses to market and state pressures
  • Membership boundaries meant that access to common resources did not extend automatically to every resident or newcomer. Swiss commoners' struggles for the right balance: Ontologies, identities and responses to market and state pressures

sections.title: What might explain it
sections.html:
Supported in case

Tying resource access to locally supportable livestock plausibly limited an individual's ability to expand grazing costs onto others. Governing the Commons: The Evolution of Institutions for Collective Action Swiss commoners' struggles for the right balance: Ontologies, identities and responses to market and state pressures

Alternative explanation: Ecological limits, household labor, and limited markets also constrained herd expansion, making the grazing rule's separate contribution difficult to establish.

Plausible

Durable commons may need to renegotiate their relationships with markets and public authorities as well as maintain their own rules. Swiss commoners' struggles for the right balance: Ontologies, identities and responses to market and state pressures

Alternative explanation: Continuing local obligations and ecological constraints may preserve some arrangements even as outside institutions change; their relative importance differs across places.

sections.title: Understanding the outcome
sections.html:
Ostrom's common-pool resource governance, qualified by historical political ecology

Boundaries and fitted rules can support coordination while leaving distributional and power questions unresolved. Governing the Commons: The Evolution of Institutions for Collective Action Swiss commoners' struggles for the right balance: Ontologies, identities and responses to market and state pressures

A membership rule that protects a resource can be exclusionary; institutional survival does not establish an ethically acceptable franchise.

sections.title: Questions to take into practice
sections.html:
• Grazing rights were connected to household capacity and collective maintenance, making access depend on obligations as well as ownership.
  • A well-maintained commons can still exclude people from benefits or a voice in its rules.
  • Private holdings and shared resources can support one another rather than requiring a wholly private or wholly communal economy.

sections.title: What remains uncertain
sections.html:
• The historical arrangement does not settle how Törbel's present-day resource use and participation have changed with markets, labor availability, and public policy.
  • The extent to which excluded households bore costs or found alternative access is important to judging the distribution of benefits.

title: Valencia: local water justice backed by wider authority
question: How do user institutions combine local knowledge with public legal recognition?
period: Historical irrigation institutions; UNESCO recognition in 2009 and historical reassessment in 2015
summary: Valencian irrigation communities developed arrangements for allocating scarce water and resolving disputes. The Water Tribunal is a visible part of this wider system, recognized in Spanish law and associated with elected irrigator representatives. Local institutions interacted with municipal and higher authorities; their long history included changes in property, membership, and political power.
outcome_summary: User institutions endured and retained meaningful local autonomy within a wider legal order. That continuity does not establish that irrigators always had equal power: claims of uniformly peasant, democratic, and unchanged governance across the thirteenth to eighteenth centuries remain contested.

sections.title: What happened
sections.html:
Mixed outcomes. User institutions endured and retained meaningful local autonomy within a wider legal order. That continuity does not establish that irrigators always had equal power: claims of uniformly peasant, democratic, and unchanged governance across the thirteenth to eighteenth centuries remain contested.

  • Irrigators' tribunals, including Valencia's Water Tribunal, have legal recognition, elected members, and oral dispute-settlement procedures. Irrigators' tribunals of the Spanish Mediterranean coast
  • Irrigation communities exercised local autonomy while interacting with municipal and higher authorities. Valencian vegetable gardens: the imperative need to update Maass, Glick and Ostrom's postulates
  • Claims that the thirteenth-to-eighteenth-century institutions were uniformly peasant, democratic, or unchanged remain historically contested. Valencian vegetable gardens: the imperative need to update Maass, Glick and Ostrom's postulates

sections.title: What might explain it
sections.html:
Plausible

Locally knowledgeable dispute resolution, backed by legal recognition, plausibly lowers the difficulty of enforcing irrigation agreements. Irrigators' tribunals of the Spanish Mediterranean coast Valencian vegetable gardens: the imperative need to update Maass, Glick and Ostrom's postulates

Alternative explanation: Landownership power and public authorities' coercive capacity may also sustain compliance without equal influence among users.

Supported in case

The institutional history may be better understood as recurrent adaptation than as preservation of a single ancient blueprint. Valencian vegetable gardens: the imperative need to update Maass, Glick and Ostrom's postulates

Alternative explanation: Some procedural continuities may remain important even when membership, property relations, and surrounding government change.

sections.title: Understanding the outcome
sections.html:
Nested commons governance in the Maass–Glick–Ostrom tradition

Local self-organization and larger-scale authority can complement each other. Valencian vegetable gardens: the imperative need to update Maass, Glick and Ostrom's postulates

Legal recognition and long survival leave separate questions about who could bring a claim, whose interests shaped decisions, and whether judgments distributed water fairly.

sections.title: Questions to take into practice
sections.html:
• Local dispute settlement can depend on recognition and enforcement beyond the community itself.
  • A continuing procedure can operate through major changes in who owns land and who holds influence.
  • Elected irrigator representatives do not by themselves reveal the position of tenants, smallholders, or users outside the recognized membership.

sections.title: What remains uncertain
sections.html:
• How accessible, timely, and impartial the tribunal is for different present-day users remains a separate question from its historical endurance.
  • Changes in landownership and representation make it difficult to infer a continuous distribution of power from the survival of a named institution.

title: Alanya: taking turns at the best fishing spots
question: When can a lottery and rotation replace competition for a scarce location?
summary: Alanya's small-boat fishers faced a narrow band of productive net-setting locations. They developed a locally agreed system that named sites, assigned starting positions by lot, and rotated access. The arrangement addressed interference and competition among participating fishers; it was not a comprehensive solution to every source of pressure on marine stocks.
outcome_summary: The historical account describes workable coordination and more evenly shared access to valuable sites. Its scope was limited: outside recreational users lacked equivalent rules, legal exclusion powers were uncertain, and informal enforcement included coercive pressure. Favorable coastal geography also reduced interference from trawlers, complicating any claim that the rules alone caused success.

sections.title: What happened
sections.html:
Mixed outcomes. The historical account describes workable coordination and more evenly shared access to valuable sites. Its scope was limited: outside recreational users lacked equivalent rules, legal exclusion powers were uncertain, and informal enforcement included coercive pressure. Favorable coastal geography also reduced interference from trawlers, complicating any claim that the rules alone caused success.

  • Licensed local fishers could join the allocation regardless of cooperative membership; a lottery established starting positions and rotation shared valuable sites. Success and Failure in Marine Coastal Fisheries of Turkey (in Making the Commons Work)
  • The agreement was deposited with local authorities, but fishers doubted they could legally remove a violator's access; informal pressure was important. Success and Failure in Marine Coastal Fisheries of Turkey (in Making the Commons Work)
  • The local allocation arrangement addressed participating small-boat fishers' use of sites, while competition involving other fishing sectors exceeded that agreement's boundaries. Local-level management and the commons problem: A comparative study of Turkish coastal fisheries

sections.title: What might explain it
sections.html:
Supported in case

Rotation made accepting a less desirable site today more tolerable by offering future access to better sites. Success and Failure in Marine Coastal Fisheries of Turkey (in Making the Commons Work)

Alternative explanation: Small-group familiarity and the ability to observe neighboring nets may have been equally important to compliance.

Plausible

The arrangement's apparent success partly depended on a problem boundary favorable to local control. Local-level management and the commons problem: A comparative study of Turkish coastal fisheries Success and Failure in Marine Coastal Fisheries of Turkey (in Making the Commons Work)

Alternative explanation: Other fishing communities might develop broader agreements; heterogeneous users do not make coordination inherently impossible.

sections.title: Understanding the outcome
sections.html:
Common-pool resource appropriation rules and conditional local self-governance

Sharing opportunities over time can reduce a scramble for a spatially scarce resource. Local-level management and the commons problem: A comparative study of Turkish coastal fisheries

More orderly site allocation does not establish sustainable fish stocks. It also leaves questions about excluded users and coercive methods of securing compliance.

sections.title: Questions to take into practice
sections.html:
• Rotation let participants accept a poor location today because their turn at better sites would come later.
  • The fishers could coordinate access to net-setting sites without controlling every source of pressure on fish stocks.
  • Informal enforcement included pressure whose fairness and legitimacy matter separately from whether the allocation system functioned.

sections.title: What remains uncertain
sections.html:
• Whether the rotation persisted under later changes in fishing pressure, membership, and coastal use is unresolved.
  • The historical allocation account does not establish the resulting condition of fish stocks or whether excluded users benefited or lost access.

title: Montreal Protocol: rules, finance, and measurements that can expose cheating
question: How can international cooperation combine obligations with assistance and independent feedback?
period: 1987–2022 assessment; unexpected emissions episode in the 2010s
summary: The Montreal Protocol connected controls on ozone-depleting substances with scientific assessment and financial assistance for eligible developing countries. Its social architecture includes differentiated obligations and a fund for compliance costs. Atmospheric measurements supplied an external check on reported activity, including evidence of unexpected emissions that complicated the otherwise strong record of reducing controlled substances.
outcome_summary: By the 2022 assessment, controlled ozone-depleting substances were declining and ozone recovery was progressing. Unexpected CFC-11 emissions showed that agreed phase-outs had not eliminated noncompliance. Subsequent declines were encouraging, but observing-network gaps and emissions from stored chemicals continued to complicate judgments about complete compliance and recovery timing.

sections.title: What happened
sections.html:
Bounded success. By the 2022 assessment, controlled ozone-depleting substances were declining and ozone recovery was progressing. Unexpected CFC-11 emissions showed that agreed phase-outs had not eliminated noncompliance. Subsequent declines were encouraging, but observing-network gaps and emissions from stored chemicals continued to complicate judgments about complete compliance and recovery timing.

  • Article 10 establishes financial and technical cooperation, including a Multilateral Fund covering agreed incremental costs for eligible parties. Montreal Protocol Article 10: Financial mechanism
  • Atmospheric measurements showed declining controlled ozone-depleting substances and progress toward ozone recovery. Scientific Assessment of Ozone Depletion 2022: Executive Summary
  • Unexpected CFC-11 emissions triggered investigations and subsequently declined, while gaps in monitoring left uncertainty about emissions elsewhere. Scientific Assessment of Ozone Depletion 2022: Executive Summary

sections.title: What might explain it
sections.html:
Plausible

Financial assistance plausibly made compliance more feasible and politically acceptable where transition costs otherwise threatened participation. Montreal Protocol Article 10: Financial mechanism

Alternative explanation: Available substitutes, commercial incentives, and domestic regulation also supported phase-outs; the financial mechanism operated alongside these changes.

Supported in case

Independent atmospheric measurement allowed the regime to detect problems that production reports alone could miss. Scientific Assessment of Ozone Depletion 2022: Executive Summary

Alternative explanation: Detection does not by itself explain subsequent reductions; enforcement, publicity, and producer decisions may have jointly contributed.

sections.title: Questions to take into practice
sections.html:
• Shared obligations became more feasible when the agreement also addressed eligible countries' transition costs.
  • Atmospheric measurements provided a check beyond countries' production reports.
  • Unexpected emissions required investigation and response after the treaty was already operating; signing an agreement was not the end of coordination.

sections.title: What remains uncertain
sections.html:
• Observing-network gaps leave uncertainty about the location and scale of some emissions.
  • Stored chemicals can continue to leak after new production is controlled, so phase-out dates and atmospheric recovery dates need not coincide.
  • The relative contributions of finance, substitutes, commercial incentives, and domestic enforcement remain difficult to separate.

title: Alaska fishing quotas: ending the race while narrowing entry
question: How can a rule improve operations while redistributing access across people and generations?
location: Alaska halibut and sablefish fisheries, United States
summary: Alaska's individual fishing quota program assigned shares of allowable harvest, replacing a compressed competitive season with more individually planned fishing. Designers added protections intended to retain small vessels, working owners, crews, and coastal communities. Over time, fishing became less compressed while access to quota and participation in the fleet consolidated.
outcome_summary: Fishing seasons lengthened and some conditions improved for remaining crews. Quota ownership and vessel participation consolidated, with unequal consequences across communities and generations. Entry barriers and transfer provisions mattered alongside changing catches and prices; the program did not produce one uniform experience for everyone formerly connected to the fisheries.

sections.title: What happened
sections.html:
Mixed outcomes. Fishing seasons lengthened and some conditions improved for remaining crews. Quota ownership and vessel participation consolidated, with unequal consequences across communities and generations. Entry barriers and transfer provisions mattered alongside changing catches and prices; the program did not produce one uniform experience for everyone formerly connected to the fisheries.

  • Fishing shifted from very short seasons to seasons lasting more than eight months. The Pacific Halibut and Sablefish Individual Fishing Quota Program: A Twenty-year Retrospective
  • Conditions improved for some remaining crews, while access and benefits became uneven across generations and communities despite protective provisions. The Pacific Halibut and Sablefish Individual Fishing Quota Program: A Twenty-year Retrospective
  • Fleet and quota-holder consolidation continued through the period reviewed in 2024, alongside changes in environmental conditions, catch limits, prices, and ownership caps. Sablefish and Halibut IFQ Review Report

sections.title: What might explain it
sections.html:
Supported in case

Secure individual allocations reduced incentives to rush for a common seasonal catch before competitors took it. The Pacific Halibut and Sablefish Individual Fishing Quota Program: A Twenty-year Retrospective

Alternative explanation: Other operational regulations and market changes also influenced timing and safety, so the changes cannot be assigned entirely to individual quota allocations.

Supported in case

Transferable rights and valuable scarce quotas can shift access toward capital and away from new entrants even when total harvest is controlled. The Pacific Halibut and Sablefish Individual Fishing Quota Program: A Twenty-year Retrospective Sablefish and Halibut IFQ Review Report

Alternative explanation: Declining catch availability and rising operating costs can make entry harder independently of ownership rules.

sections.title: Understanding the outcome
sections.html:
Catch-share incentives versus distributional objectives

A rule addressing the race to fish simultaneously creates assets whose allocation affects livelihoods. The Pacific Halibut and Sablefish Individual Fishing Quota Program: A Twenty-year Retrospective Sablefish and Halibut IFQ Review Report

Reduced vessel numbers are neither automatically a social failure nor proof of healthy fish stocks; affected groups and ecological outcomes need distinct measures.

sections.title: Questions to take into practice
sections.html:
• Initial quota allocation created valuable assets, making later entry a different problem from the original allocation.
  • Improved conditions among remaining participants can coexist with lost access for people who leave or cannot enter.
  • Protective ownership and vessel rules need to be judged by their effects across communities, not only by whether they exist.

sections.title: What remains uncertain
sections.html:
• Quota ownership, changing catch availability, and rising operating costs all affected entry; their separate contributions are difficult to establish.
  • Longer seasons and fewer vessels describe operational changes, not a demonstrated quota-caused recovery of biological stocks.

title: New Zealand quotas: owning fishing assets is not the same as being able to fish
question: When do formally allocated rights fail to translate into practical access or self-determination?
period: 1986 quota system; 1992 settlement and subsequent development examined through 2024
summary: New Zealand's quota system divides allowable commercial harvest into shares and annual catch entitlements. Its development intersected with Māori rights claims and a settlement transferring assets and governance powers. The case distinguishes a formal allocation from the practical ability to use it.
outcome_summary: The system limits and allocates catches, and Māori entities acquired valuable assets. Yet small-scale fishers continued to face regulatory and market barriers. Collective ownership of quota therefore did not necessarily translate into fishing livelihoods for particular households, and neither measure alone establishes ecological recovery or self-determination.

sections.title: What happened
sections.html:
Mixed outcomes. The system limits and allocates catches, and Māori entities acquired valuable assets. Yet small-scale fishers continued to face regulatory and market barriers. Collective ownership of quota therefore did not necessarily translate into fishing livelihoods for particular households, and neither measure alone establishes ecological recovery or self-determination.

  • The official system allocates annual catch entitlement according to quota ownership and the commercial catch limit for a stock. Quota Management System
  • Initial allocation disadvantaged some part-time Māori fishers; later settlement arrangements transferred fishing rights and assets to Māori entities. Indigenous self-determination in fisheries governance: implications from New Zealand and Atlantic Canada
  • Regulatory and market-access constraints continued after those reallocations, limiting some fishers' ability to turn rights into practical fishing opportunities. Indigenous self-determination in fisheries governance: implications from New Zealand and Atlantic Canada

sections.title: What might explain it
sections.html:
Supported in case

Collective asset income can coexist with limited fishing opportunities for particular households. Indigenous self-determination in fisheries governance: implications from New Zealand and Atlantic Canada

Alternative explanation: Collective dividend strategies may deliberately prioritize all beneficiaries rather than maximize employment for a smaller subset of fishers.

Plausible

Tradability does not alone explain conservation gains, since limits and initial allocation changes can affect pressure before a quota market operates. Quota Management System Indigenous self-determination in fisheries governance: implications from New Zealand and Atlantic Canada

Alternative explanation: Market reallocation may still improve later efficiency; establishing that requires separating its effect from catch limits and enforcement.

sections.title: Understanding the outcome
sections.html:
Indigenous self-determination and the distinction between formal rights and access to benefits

Formal ownership and practical access are different. Indigenous self-determination in fisheries governance: implications from New Zealand and Atlantic Canada

Treaty obligations and colonial history preclude treating iwi simply as investor groups.

sections.title: Questions to take into practice
sections.html:
• An entity can hold a valuable right while individual households lack the means to use it.
  • Income from collectively owned assets, fishing work, food access, and political authority are different benefits and can move in different directions.
  • Allocation criteria can preserve historical exclusions even when they appear administratively neutral.

sections.title: What remains uncertain
sections.html:
• Biological outcomes vary by stock and cannot be inferred from the value of quota assets or their ownership.
  • Different iwi and households may experience the system differently; a single national average would conceal differences in assets, strategy, and practical access.

title: Nepal community forests: environmental gains without equal voice
question: Can decentralization reduce forest loss and poverty while leaving local elites in charge?
period: National outcomes 2000–2012; leadership research published in 2015
location: Nepal, national comparison and Baglung district leadership study
summary: Nepal transferred day-to-day forest management responsibilities to community forest user groups. Deforestation and poverty declined on average in a national comparison, while a separate examination of leadership in Baglung found executive roles dominated by relatively wealthy and higher-caste people. Environmental and livelihood gains could coexist with unequal decision power.
outcome_summary: The national analysis estimated improvements in both forest and poverty outcomes on average, with substantial variation. The Baglung study found executive roles dominated by relatively wealthy and higher-caste people. These findings are compatible: a program can improve aggregate outcomes while still reproducing inequalities in voice and access.

sections.title: What happened
sections.html:
Mixed outcomes. The national analysis estimated improvements in both forest and poverty outcomes on average, with substantial variation. The Baglung study found executive roles dominated by relatively wealthy and higher-caste people. These findings are compatible: a program can improve aggregate outcomes while still reproducing inequalities in voice and access.

  • A national analysis combining poverty, forest-change, and community-forest information estimated relative reductions of 37% in deforestation and 4.3% in poverty associated with community forestry over 2000–2012. Community forest management simultaneously reduces poverty and deforestation in Nepal
  • Benefits varied, with poorer areas less effective at reducing deforestation and larger or older community forests showing greater gains. Community forest management simultaneously reduces poverty and deforestation in Nepal
  • In Baglung, executive committees were dominated by relatively wealthy and higher-caste members. Prior NGO leadership experience was associated with greater access to these roles for disadvantaged people. How can poor and disadvantaged households get an opportunity to become a leader in community forestry in Nepal?

sections.title: What might explain it
sections.html:
Plausible

Local management authority may help users establish resource rules that fit local conditions and support joint environmental and livelihood gains. Community forest management simultaneously reduces poverty and deforestation in Nepal

Alternative explanation: Selection into community forestry and unobserved changes in livelihoods or government support could explain some estimated gains.

Supported in case

Leadership experience may help disadvantaged people cross barriers to formal decision roles. How can poor and disadvantaged households get an opportunity to become a leader in community forestry in Nepal?

Alternative explanation: People obtaining NGO experience may already differ in confidence, networks, or resources; the association does not establish a training effect.

sections.title: Understanding the outcome
sections.html:
Decentralized commons governance with distributional and elite-capture analysis

Environmental effectiveness and democratic inclusion are separate dimensions of institutional performance. Community forest management simultaneously reduces poverty and deforestation in Nepal How can poor and disadvantaged households get an opportunity to become a leader in community forestry in Nepal?

The Baglung sample cannot be treated as a census of all Nepalese user groups, nor can national averages describe every household.

sections.title: Questions to take into practice
sections.html:
• Reduced deforestation, reduced poverty, and a more inclusive leadership are different outcomes; improvement in one does not establish improvement in the others.
  • Membership and meeting attendance can coexist with leadership concentrated among advantaged people.
  • Poorer communities may need resources and support that better-established groups already possess.

sections.title: What remains uncertain
sections.html:
• Selection into community forestry and changes in livelihoods or government support may explain part of the estimated national gains.
  • The national comparison and Baglung leadership findings concern different populations and periods; they do not establish which particular groups combined environmental gains with elite control.

title: Uganda forest monitoring: watching one place can move the damage elsewhere
question: What happens when a local intervention changes where people extract resources rather than how much?
summary: Community forest monitoring was introduced in a randomized trial across Ugandan villages. Resource use was measured inside and outside monitored areas, allowing changes beyond the intervention boundary to become visible. Watching particular forest areas did not necessarily reduce the pressure on forests overall.
outcome_summary: The trial detected no improvement in its main forest-use index. Forest loss increased in unmonitored areas relative to controls, consistent with some extraction moving outside the monitored boundary, although displacement is not the only possible explanation. Across a broader six-country study including this trial, monitoring produced modest average benefits, so the Ugandan result differed from the pooled result.

sections.title: What happened
sections.html:
Failure on the stated objective. The trial detected no improvement in its main forest-use index. Forest loss increased in unmonitored areas relative to controls, consistent with some extraction moving outside the monitored boundary, although displacement is not the only possible explanation. Across a broader six-country study including this trial, monitoring produced modest average benefits, so the Ugandan result differed from the pooled result.

  • The trial randomized monitoring across 110 villages and combined ground measurements with satellite observations. Can community monitoring save the commons? Evidence on forest use and displacement
  • The main forest-use index showed no treatment effect, while unmonitored areas near treatment and neighboring villages experienced relative increases in forest loss. Can community monitoring save the commons? Evidence on forest use and displacement
  • A harmonized six-country study, which includes the Uganda experiment, found modest average improvements in resource use, knowledge, and satisfaction across settings. Adoption of community monitoring improves common pool resource management across contexts

sections.title: What might explain it
sections.html:
Plausible

Fear of sanctions may have shifted some extraction beyond monitored boundaries instead of reducing demand. Can community monitoring save the commons? Evidence on forest use and displacement

Alternative explanation: Other changes affecting unmonitored areas could have contributed to the increase. Random assignment identifies effects of the intervention more clearly than it identifies why forest loss shifted.

Plausible

Monitoring works differently when users can move pressure to nearby unobserved resources. Can community monitoring save the commons? Evidence on forest use and displacement Adoption of community monitoring improves common pool resource management across contexts

Alternative explanation: Differences in implementation, resource type, authority, or incentives may explain cross-site variation rather than spatial leakage alone.

sections.title: Understanding the outcome
sections.html:
Commons monitoring as a testable institutional component; spillover and displacement effects

A design condition can have conditional effects, and local improvement is not equivalent to net environmental improvement. Can community monitoring save the commons? Evidence on forest use and displacement Adoption of community monitoring improves common pool resource management across contexts

The trial tests a particular externally supported monitoring intervention, not a complete long-standing commons institution.

sections.title: Questions to take into practice
sections.html:
• An intervention's environmental effects can extend beyond the area where it operates; observing only the monitored forest would miss part of this result.
  • Installing a monitoring arrangement and reducing total extraction are different achievements.
  • Nearby unmonitored resources can become attractive when the risks or costs of extraction rise inside the monitored area.

sections.title: What remains uncertain
sections.html:
• Whether the increase outside monitored areas reflected displaced extraction, other behavioral changes, or additional local factors remains uncertain.
  • The durability of the effects after the trial and their consequences for households dependent on forest resources remain unresolved.

title: Sierra Juárez: winning community control did not remove market constraints
question: How do collective resource institutions emerge through political struggle rather than simply being designed?
period: 1940–1983 concessions and transition; later community management examined through 2020
summary: Sierra Juárez forest communities confronted state-supported forestry concessions and later gained greater control over management. An imposed association of communities struggled, while community mobilization and changing forestry laws helped open a route to local control. Acquiring authority was only one step: communities still had to organize production and find viable markets.
outcome_summary: Community organization helped change control over forest resources and supported durable management arrangements. Earlier imposed associations struggled with unequal exploitation and financial management. Later communities faced transport costs, market competition, and limited timber income, so stronger political control did not bring uniform commercial success.

sections.title: What happened
sections.html:
Mixed outcomes. Community organization helped change control over forest resources and supported durable management arrangements. Earlier imposed associations struggled with unequal exploitation and financial management. Later communities faced transport costs, market competition, and limited timber income, so stronger political control did not bring uniform commercial success.

  • State concessions placed forestry under FAPATUX, while an imposed association of forest communities failed amid unequal exploitation and financial-management problems. Concesiones Forestales y Empresas Comunitarias en Sierra Juárez (1940–1983). Apuestas del Estado Mexicano
  • Community mobilization, the ending of concessions, and the development of local management marked major changes in control over the region's forests. Community forest appropriation in the Sierra Juárez of Oaxaca in the face of forest policies
  • Stronger community governance coexisted with persistent production costs, transport difficulties, and limited income gains from timber and certification. Community forest appropriation in the Sierra Juárez of Oaxaca in the face of forest policies

sections.title: What might explain it
sections.html:
Supported in case

Locally grounded collective organization made it possible to contest externally assigned control and sustain management after concessions. Community forest appropriation in the Sierra Juárez of Oaxaca in the face of forest policies

Alternative explanation: Changes in national law, political opportunities, and external support also enabled the transition; organization alone was not sufficient.

Plausible

An imposed multi-community organization struggled when resource contributions and benefits differed without accepted arrangements for managing those differences. Concesiones Forestales y Empresas Comunitarias en Sierra Juárez (1940–1983). Apuestas del Estado Mexicano

Alternative explanation: Administrative weaknesses, state-company incentives, and market conditions could explain failures apart from intercommunity inequality.

sections.title: Understanding the outcome
sections.html:
Community appropriation and historically situated forest governance

Control over resources is produced through conflict, law, and collective organization, not only internal operational rules. Concesiones Forestales y Empresas Comunitarias en Sierra Juárez (1940–1983). Apuestas del Estado Mexicano Community forest appropriation in the Sierra Juárez of Oaxaca in the face of forest policies

Community land institutions and the legal history of concessions shaped which claims could succeed. Internal rules alone would not give another community equivalent authority over a resource.

sections.title: Questions to take into practice
sections.html:
• The authority to manage a resource may have to be won through political organization and legal change before local procedures can matter.
  • Control over forests and the ability to earn sustainable income from them are separate problems.
  • A multi-community organization needs accepted ways to handle unequal resource contributions and benefits.

sections.title: What remains uncertain
sections.html:
• The regional trajectory combines communities with different resources and histories; their gains and difficulties were not identical.
  • The relationship between changes in control and subsequent forest-cover outcomes remains distinct from the evidence of political and organizational change.
  • Unequal benefits, administrative weaknesses, and state-company incentives may all have contributed to the imposed association's failure.

title: Bologna: giving citizen projects a recognized relationship with city government
question: Can legal agreements turn informal care for shared places into sustained public collaboration?
summary: Bologna's 2014 regulation created a framework for citizens and the municipality to agree on caring for and regenerating urban commons. Collaboration pacts made responsibilities and support discussable within a recognized public process. The framework supported extensive participation, while delivering and sustaining environmental or economic changes remained a further challenge.
outcome_summary: More than 800 pacts were activated after 2014. By the 2026 assessment, governance and participation were more developed than environmental and economic implementation. The agreements created a durable way to organize collaboration, but their number alone did not show whether assets were maintained, benefits were distributed equally, or climate goals were achieved.

sections.title: What happened
sections.html:
Mixed outcomes. More than 800 pacts were activated after 2014. By the 2026 assessment, governance and participation were more developed than environmental and economic implementation. The agreements created a durable way to organize collaboration, but their number alone did not show whether assets were maintained, benefits were distributed equally, or climate goals were achieved.

  • The regulation defines collaboration between citizens and the municipality for the care and regeneration of tangible, intangible, and digital urban commons. Regulation on Collaboration between Citizens and the City for the Care and Regeneration of Urban Commons
  • More than 800 pacts had been activated since 2014, and the collaboration arrangements had connections to Bologna's climate-contract work by 2026. The City as a Commons Approach and New Forms of Collaborative Governance Models: The Example of Bologna
  • The qualitative and indicator-based assessment found environmental and economic implementation less developed than governance and participation; it identified a pattern rather than a causal effect of the pacts. The City as a Commons Approach and New Forms of Collaborative Governance Models: The Example of Bologna

sections.title: What might explain it
sections.html:
Plausible

A recognized agreement framework plausibly reduces uncertainty about how officials and citizen groups can work together. Regulation on Collaboration between Citizens and the City for the Care and Regeneration of Urban Commons

Alternative explanation: Bologna's existing civic organizations and administrative capacity may explain much of the observed collaboration.

Supported in case

Participation infrastructure can expand faster than the money, technical capability, and maintenance needed for downstream outcomes. The City as a Commons Approach and New Forms of Collaborative Governance Models: The Example of Bologna

Alternative explanation: Some environmental effects may take longer to appear or may not be captured by the indicators used.

sections.title: Understanding the outcome
sections.html:
City as a Commons and collaborative urban governance

Government provided a recognized framework for residents to share stewardship, rather than acting only as an owner or purchaser of services. The City as a Commons Approach and New Forms of Collaborative Governance Models: The Example of Bologna

Unpaid participation requires time and resources that residents possess unequally. A pact can add civic capacity, but it can also shift work onto residents that a public service would otherwise provide.

sections.title: Questions to take into practice
sections.html:
• An agreement to begin work needs resources, maintenance responsibilities, and a way to handle withdrawal if it is to sustain a shared place.
  • Signed pacts show that collaboration is taking place; completed and maintained outcomes reveal what it delivers.
  • The distribution of unpaid work matters when judging whether collaboration adds capacity or transfers public obligations to residents.

sections.title: What remains uncertain
sections.html:
• The persistence and quality of maintenance across individual pacts remain different questions from the number activated.
  • Environmental changes may take longer to appear or fall outside the chosen indicators, complicating comparisons with participation outcomes.
  • How unpaid labor, municipal support, and benefits are distributed across neighborhoods remains unresolved.

title: Chile: an inclusive drafting process still had to persuade the electorate
question: How can a constitution-making process lose the consent needed to enact its result?
period: 2021–2023, focusing on the 2022 proposal and its rejection
summary: Chile elected a constitutional convention and subjected its proposed replacement constitution to a national referendum. The process expanded representation and participation in drafting, but the electorate rejected the 2022 text. A differently organized second process also ended in rejection in 2023, making it difficult to reduce the episode to one procedural flaw or ideological explanation.
outcome_summary: Both processes ended without an enacted replacement constitution. Voters rejected the texts through the final decision assigned to them: 61.86% voted to reject in the final preliminary 2022 tally, and 55.76% voted against the second proposal in the equivalent 2023 bulletin. Fragmented drafting and difficult bargaining may help explain the first result, but the second rejection under a different process makes a single procedural explanation inadequate.

sections.title: What happened
sections.html:
Failure on the stated objective. Both processes ended without an enacted replacement constitution. Voters rejected the texts through the final decision assigned to them: 61.86% voted to reject in the final preliminary 2022 tally, and 55.76% voted against the second proposal in the equivalent 2023 bulletin. Fragmented drafting and difficult bargaining may help explain the first result, but the second rejection under a different process makes a single procedural explanation inadequate.

  • Servel's final preliminary 2022 tally reported 61.86% voting to reject the convention's proposal. Servel realiza balance del Plebiscito Constitucional
  • The first convention combined party-less independents, a comparatively weak right-wing bloc, and decentralized public drafting. How not to write a constitution: lessons from Chile
  • Servel's final preliminary 2023 bulletin reported 55.76% voting against the second proposal. Boletín final sobre resultados preliminares del Plebiscito Constitucional 2023

sections.title: What might explain it
sections.html:
Contested

Weak coordination and limited cross-bloc bargaining may have produced a draft insufficiently aligned with a wider electorate. How not to write a constitution: lessons from Chile

Alternative explanation: Substantive opposition to provisions, campaign dynamics, distrust, and changing turnout could produce rejection even under a more coordinated process.

Plausible

Representativeness inside a convention does not automatically create a durable ratification coalition outside it. How not to write a constitution: lessons from Chile Servel realiza balance del Plebiscito Constitucional Boletín final sobre resultados preliminares del Plebiscito Constitucional 2023

Alternative explanation: A sufficiently popular substantive package might win without strong party coordination; this case does not isolate either mechanism.

sections.title: Understanding the outcome
sections.html:
Constitution-making rules, political contingency, and negotiated consent

Procedures shape bargaining incentives, but their effects depend on the actors and political moment. How not to write a constitution: lessons from Chile

A rejected text does not reveal which alternative procedure would have secured approval. More coordination among political leaders could change bargaining without necessarily making the result more legitimate.

sections.title: Questions to take into practice
sections.html:
• A convention's ability to produce a text and its ability to assemble a wider ratification coalition are separate achievements.
  • Rejection of a proposed constitution can be an exercise of democratic participation rather than its failure.
  • The people represented in drafting and the electorate deciding adoption may differ in turnout, priorities, and political alignment.

sections.title: What remains uncertain
sections.html:
• The relative contributions of disputed provisions, campaign dynamics, trust, turnout, and drafting arrangements remain contested.
  • The two rejections do not establish an ideal degree of transparency or party control in constitution-making.

title: Andhra Pradesh: exposing corruption was not the same as deterring it
question: What must connect public scrutiny to consequences for wrongdoing?
period: Social audits institutionalized from 2006; evaluations published in 2014–2015
location: Andhra Pradesh, India, under the boundaries and program arrangements studied
summary: Andhra Pradesh institutionalized social audits of a rural employment program, allowing beneficiaries and auditors to inspect records and raise irregularities publicly. The audits made wrongdoing more visible, but exposure was not reliably connected to consequences. Officials could adapt to scrutiny, leaving a gap between detecting irregularities and deterring them.
outcome_summary: Audits detected irregularities and showed evidence of beneficiary learning, with a modest reduction in leakage per labor-related irregularity. Repeated audits did not deter irregularities overall, and material-related problems increased. Public scrutiny created information, but the evaluated system did not consistently convert that information into prevention or effective accountability.

sections.title: What happened
sections.html:
Mixed outcomes. Audits detected irregularities and showed evidence of beneficiary learning, with a modest reduction in leakage per labor-related irregularity. Repeated audits did not deter irregularities overall, and material-related problems increased. Public scrutiny created information, but the evaluated system did not consistently convert that information into prevention or effective accountability.

  • Andhra Pradesh established formally organized, recurring social audits of employment-program works from 2006. A Guide to Conducting Social Audits
  • The panel analysis detected no statistically significant employment-generation effect and estimated a modest decline in leakage per labor-related irregularity. Social audits and MGNREGA Delivery: Lessons from Andhra Pradesh
  • Material-related irregularities increased, and repeated audits did not produce overall deterrence. Social audits and MGNREGA Delivery: Lessons from Andhra Pradesh

sections.title: What might explain it
sections.html:
Supported in case

When detection is not followed by credible consequences, officials can learn to shift irregularities toward less visible or less beneficiary-sensitive channels. Social audits and MGNREGA Delivery: Lessons from Andhra Pradesh

Alternative explanation: Changes in reporting or audit skill may alter measured irregularities without equivalent changes in underlying corruption.

Plausible

Beneficiary involvement may improve scrutiny most where participants directly understand what they should receive. A Guide to Conducting Social Audits Social audits and MGNREGA Delivery: Lessons from Andhra Pradesh

Alternative explanation: Different transaction complexity, documentation, and auditor expertise could explain the contrast between labor and material irregularities.

sections.title: Understanding the outcome
sections.html:
Social accountability as an information–response chain, with strategic adaptation

Voice and information are intermediate outputs; deterrence also requires enforceable responsibility for responding. Social audits and MGNREGA Delivery: Lessons from Andhra Pradesh A Guide to Conducting Social Audits

The pattern concerns one program and period. Consequences after detection, the complexity of transactions, and beneficiaries' ability to recognize problems all affect what public scrutiny can accomplish.

sections.title: Questions to take into practice
sections.html:
• Public findings need an actor responsible for correction and a deadline for responding; otherwise exposure can leave the underlying incentives unchanged.
  • Meetings and complaints reveal activity, while recovery, correction, and repeated offenses reveal what follows from it.
  • Officials can adapt to scrutiny by moving irregularities toward transactions that beneficiaries find harder to observe.

sections.title: What remains uncertain
sections.html:
• Improved detection can increase recorded irregularities even if underlying corruption does not rise, complicating interpretation of the observed changes.
  • Longer-term deterrence and the consequences of participation for complainants remain unresolved.

title: Ansari XPRIZE: a winning flight is not an industry
question: What can a prize accomplish when developing the winning invention costs more than the reward?
summary: The Ansari XPRIZE offered $10 million for a privately funded spacecraft that could reach space twice within two weeks. Paul Allen financed Burt Rutan’s team to build SpaceShipOne, which won in 2004. The reward gave the team a public target, but a wealthy backer made the attempt possible. Turning the achievement into a commercial passenger service took much longer.
outcome_summary: The team achieved the flight target and its technology was licensed to Virgin Galactic. The demonstration succeeded; commercial service followed in 2023, after a separate development program. The prize alone could neither pay for the winning project nor carry it through that transition.

sections.title: The prize did not pay for the attempt
sections.html:
A prize competition offers a reward after success. The team still has to find the money to begin—and absorb the loss if it fails. SpaceShipOne had a backer able to take that risk: Paul Allen. In his memoir, he put the project’s cost at $28 million, nearly three times the $10 million reward.

That makes patronage part of the explanation. The competition supplied a target and recognition; Allen supplied resources that made an attempt possible. A team with a promising idea but no comparable backing would face a very different challenge.

The prize may have focused effort on a visible, testable achievement. How much new effort it created is harder to establish: Allen’s interest in rocketry and Rutan’s engineering ambitions also mattered. Their success cannot tell us what they would have built without the competition.

sections.title: A winning flight is a beginning
sections.html:
SpaceShipOne won in 2004. Against the stated flight challenge, the competition succeeded. But proving that a vehicle can make qualifying flights leaves substantial work before it can support an ongoing passenger service.

Virgin Galactic licensed the technology; its first commercial service mission followed in 2023. That nineteen-year interval involved a separate development program. The winning demonstration had not, by itself, supplied everything needed to operate a business.

The distinction matters when designing a prize. A clear finish line can concentrate attention and effort. Work beyond that finish line—further development, reliable operations, and finding customers—needs people and funding of its own. The achievement here was real; treating it as the creation of a functioning industry would hide much of the work still ahead.

title: Google Lunar XPRIZE: no winner, unfinished trajectories
question: Can an inducement prize fail its deadline yet leave useful capabilities behind?
summary: Google Lunar XPRIZE challenged private teams to reach the Moon and perform specified operations. After repeated development efforts, the organizer announced that the final deadline would pass without a grand-prize winner. One continuing entrant, SpaceIL, subsequently reached lunar orbit but lost its lander during descent, separating organizational persistence from completion.
outcome_summary: No team met the competition’s deadline. SpaceIL later reached lunar orbit but did not land successfully: a team and its capabilities survived the award, while the original objective remained unmet.

sections.title: What happened
sections.html:
Failure on the stated objective. No team met the competition’s deadline. SpaceIL later reached lunar orbit but did not land successfully: a team and its capabilities survived the award, while the original objective remained unmet.

  • In January 2018 the organizer said no finalist would attempt launch by the March 31 deadline and the grand prize would remain unclaimed. An Important Update From Google Lunar XPRIZE
  • The organizer attributed delay to fundraising, engineering, and regulatory difficulties; it also reported milestone payments exceeding $6 million. An Important Update From Google Lunar XPRIZE
  • SpaceIL was established for the competition, continued after its end, and reached lunar orbit before losing its lander during the April 2019 descent. Beresheet

sections.title: What might explain it
sections.html:
Plausible

Back-loaded payment may have been poorly matched to expensive development and launch dependencies. An Important Update From Google Lunar XPRIZE

Alternative explanation: Even with advance grants, the same engineering or regulatory bottlenecks might have prevented a timely landing.

Participant explanation

The competition may have helped form teams whose work outlived the cash award. An Important Update From Google Lunar XPRIZE Beresheet

Alternative explanation: Independent national aspirations, philanthropy, and later institutional support may explain continuation better than the prize.

sections.title: Questions to take into practice
sections.html:
• Define in advance how deadline failure differs from learning, team formation, and later procurement outcomes.
  • Compare a final purse with staged grants when teams face large costs before demonstration.

sections.title: What remains uncertain
sections.html: • It remains unclear how much entrant investment depended on the prize. SpaceIL’s continuation also leaves open what happened to the less visible teams and their work.

title: Carbon Removal XPRIZE: awarded, not climate-scale proof
question: What does a judged removal demonstration establish about a proposed climate intervention?
location: International competition; Mati deployment in India
summary: The $100 million Carbon Removal XPRIZE concluded in 2025 with Mati Carbon winning the grand prize for enhanced weathering. Teams had to turn proposed removal methods into evaluated demonstrations. The award made their work more visible, but expanding a demonstration into economical removal at climate-relevant scale requires further evidence about cost, production and storage.
outcome_summary: The competition awarded its prizes, and Mati subsequently received a verified credit issuance. Those are milestones in demonstration and certification. Deployment at gigatonne scale and storage lasting centuries remain substantially larger claims.

sections.title: What happened
sections.html:
Mixed outcomes. The competition awarded its prizes, and Mati subsequently received a verified credit issuance. Those are milestones in demonstration and certification. Deployment at gigatonne scale and storage lasting centuries remain substantially larger claims.

  • Mati won the grand prize; three runners-up and separate XFACTOR awards recognized other approaches. XPRIZE Carbon Removal Competition
  • Mati received the $50 million grand prize in April 2025, with scientific leadership connected to Yale. Yale-Related Nonprofit Wins $50 Million XPRIZE Carbon Removal
  • Isometric records 209.08 certificates issued to Mati on June 17, 2026, naming Earthood as verifier and Enhanced Weathering in Agriculture v1.2 as protocol. 209.08 certificates issued to Mati

sections.title: What might explain it
sections.html:
Plausible

A common demonstration requirement may make otherwise dissimilar removal approaches easier for funders to compare. XPRIZE Carbon Removal Competition

Alternative explanation: Selection may mostly identify teams already advantaged by capital, research partnerships, and measurement infrastructure.

Plausible

Certification can create a transaction-ready signal before society can directly observe the full claimed storage period. 209.08 certificates issued to Mati

Alternative explanation: That signal depends on protocol assumptions and verification; buyers may instead rely primarily on institutional reputation or contractual protection.

sections.title: Questions to take into practice
sections.html:
• Keep measured removal, modeled durability, credits issued, and credits sold as separate quantities.
  • Ask what follow-up evidence would change confidence after judges announce a winner.

sections.title: What remains uncertain
sections.html: • The 209.08-certificate registry transaction covers a particular issuance, not the competition’s total measured removal. Long-run costs and storage durability remain questions beyond that transaction and the award.

title: Netflix Prize: winning the metric, missing production
question: How can a competition succeed technically without its winning system being deployed?
summary: Netflix offered $1 million for a ten-percent improvement in a movie-rating prediction metric. The challenge was won, but the final ensemble was not deployed as a complete production system. Earlier competition methods were used. Meanwhile, streaming changed the product, available behavioral data, and what a useful recommendation needed to accomplish.
outcome_summary: The benchmark target was met and earlier competition techniques entered production. Netflix’s engineers judged the final ensemble’s additional accuracy insufficient to justify its integration cost. Useful research emerged even though the complete winning system was not adopted.

sections.title: What happened
sections.html:
Mixed outcomes. The benchmark target was met and earlier competition techniques entered production. Netflix’s engineers judged the final ensemble’s additional accuracy insufficient to justify its integration cost. Useful research emerged even though the complete winning system was not adopted.

  • The contest scored errors in predicted movie ratings, using that measurable task as a proxy for the broader problem of recommending something a viewer would enjoy. Netflix Recommendations: Beyond the 5 stars, Part 1
  • They reported deploying two earlier methods after adaptation, but judged the final ensemble’s additional gains insufficient for its production engineering cost. Netflix Recommendations: Beyond the 5 stars, Part 1
  • Converting viewers’ ratings into a common score let competitors optimize a technical target, while leaving other aspects of cultural preference outside the benchmark. Recommended for you: The Netflix Prize and the production of algorithmic culture

sections.title: What might explain it
sections.html:
Supported in case

A fixed benchmark can reward complexity whose integration costs are absent from the scoring rule. Netflix Recommendations: Beyond the 5 stars, Part 1

Alternative explanation: A simpler winning system could still have become obsolete because Netflix’s business and interaction data changed.

Plausible

The competition may have been valuable as distributed research even when the final artifact was unsuitable. Netflix Recommendations: Beyond the 5 stars, Part 1 Recommended for you: The Netflix Prize and the production of algorithmic culture

Alternative explanation: Similar research might have emerged internally or publicly without the tournament; benefits must be compared with participant and organizer costs.

sections.title: Understanding the outcome
sections.html:
Algorithmic culture, Hallinan and Striphas

The metric operationalized one interpretation of audience preference and success. Recommended for you: The Netflix Prize and the production of algorithmic culture

Predicting a rating is narrower than helping someone choose what to watch; the cultural interpretation alone cannot tell us whether a different funding method would have worked better.

sections.title: Questions to take into practice
sections.html:
• Include deployment constraints and changing product requirements in an evaluation plan.
  • Track intermediate knowledge transfers separately from adoption of the final winning artifact.

sections.title: What remains uncertain
sections.html: • The competition’s net value depends on organizer and entrant costs as well as useful techniques. Netflix’s engineers explained their deployment decision, but the comparable cost and output of an internal research program remain uncertain.

title: DARPA Grand Challenge: zero finishers, then five
question: When should a failed challenge be repeated rather than abandoned?
summary: DARPA’s first desert-driving challenge offered a public test and prize for autonomous vehicles. Nobody finished in 2004. The agency repeated the contest in 2005 with a larger purse, and five vehicles completed the course. An unsuccessful first test became a starting point for another round of engineering rather than the end of the program.
outcome_summary: The second event achieved the specified demonstration, with multiple finishers rather than a lone exceptional entrant. This is success at autonomous desert traversal; it is not evidence that the same systems were ready for unrestricted public-road service.

sections.title: What happened
sections.html:
Bounded success. The second event achieved the specified demonstration, with multiple finishers rather than a lone exceptional entrant. This is success at autonomous desert traversal; it is not evidence that the same systems were ready for unrestricted public-road service.

  • No vehicle finished in 2004. Five finished in 2005, when Stanford won the $2 million award. Grand Challenge
  • Registrations rose from 107 in 2004 to 195 in 2005; smaller numbers qualified for the races themselves. Stanley: The robot that won the DARPA Grand Challenge
  • The technical paper attributes Stanley’s performance to an integrated development effort involving perception, planning, control, machine learning, testing, and several institutional partners. Stanley: The robot that won the DARPA Grand Challenge

sections.title: What might explain it
sections.html:
Plausible

A repeatable public test may coordinate complementary engineering work around a shared definition of progress. Grand Challenge Stanley: The robot that won the DARPA Grand Challenge

Alternative explanation: Extra development time, accumulated research, and improved hardware could explain improvement even without a competition.

Plausible

Retaining the challenge after failure may allow learning that a one-shot award would lose. Stanley: The robot that won the DARPA Grand Challenge

Alternative explanation: The second event changed entrants, purse, and course; it is not a controlled comparison of persistence alone.

sections.title: Questions to take into practice
sections.html:
• Before repeating a challenge, ask whether the first attempt revealed tractable bottlenecks or an unrealistic target.
  • Preserve evaluation data and technical accounts so failure can inform the next round.

sections.title: What remains uncertain
sections.html: • The second round changed the purse, course and entrants while allowing more development time, so the improvement cannot be attributed to the larger reward alone. The costs and learning of unsuccessful entrants are also needed to assess the program’s wider value.

title: Longitude: the prize that was also a funding institution
question: Was the celebrated longitude breakthrough really a winner-takes-all prize?
summary: The longitude problem is often told as one outsider solving a problem and claiming a reward. The actual arrangement included a board, tests, repeated development payments, disclosure disputes, and later manufacturing improvements. Harrison’s accurate timekeeper did not automatically settle questions about practicality or the terms under which public money should be paid.
outcome_summary: Marine timekeeping advanced through interim funding, contested evaluation and later manufacturing improvements. Harrison’s reward remained disputed, and an accurate instrument still had to become a design others could reproduce and use.

sections.title: What happened
sections.html:
Mixed outcomes. Marine timekeeping advanced through interim funding, contested evaluation and later manufacturing improvements. Harrison’s reward remained disputed, and an accurate instrument still had to become a design others could reproduce and use.

  • Harrison’s H4 met the accuracy standard, but the Board questioned its practicality and withheld the full reward. Board of Longitude Inventors: John Harrison
  • Substantial interim payments helped fund development, followed by a long trajectory of further chronometer invention, manufacturing improvements and patenting. Prizes, patents and the search for longitude
  • Their analysis finds progress payments did not predict inventor entry or patent timing, despite helping finance particular inventors. Prizes, patents and the search for longitude

sections.title: What might explain it
sections.html:
Plausible

The board’s continuing finance and evaluation may have mattered as much as the headline reward. Board of Longitude Inventors: John Harrison Prizes, patents and the search for longitude

Alternative explanation: Private markets and naval demand could have driven cumulative improvement even with a different funding institution.

Plausible

Disclosure and reproducibility requirements may explain some conflict that a heroic-inventor story treats simply as obstruction. Prizes, patents and the search for longitude Board of Longitude Inventors: John Harrison

Alternative explanation: Officials could also have exercised inconsistent judgment or protected preferred approaches; practicality concerns do not prove neutral administration.

sections.title: Understanding the outcome
sections.html:
Complementarity of prizes, patents, and cumulative innovation

Payments, disclosure requirements and later manufacturing improvements worked together; a headline prize did not supply the whole path from invention to widespread use. Prizes, patents and the search for longitude

Later patent comparisons do not isolate the original 1714 reward or establish one optimal policy.

sections.title: Questions to take into practice
sections.html:
• Specify whether a reward requires a demonstration, reproducible design, economical manufacture, or all three.
  • Compare staged support and knowledge disclosure with a pure final-payout design.

sections.title: What remains uncertain
sections.html: • Historical records disproportionately preserve prominent inventors. Exact causal contributions of public payments, market demand, patents, and skilled craft networks remain difficult to separate.

title: Orteig Prize: the famous winner and the missing entrants
question: What disappears when a prize is remembered only through its winner?
summary: The Orteig offer rewarded a nonstop flight between New York and Paris. Charles Lindbergh won in 1927 with financial backing from St. Louis businessmen. The familiar story of a clear target and celebrated breakthrough also contains less visible unsuccessful attempts, including the disappearance of Charles Nungesser during his bid.
outcome_summary: The specified flight was achieved and publicly celebrated. Other entrants faced catastrophic losses. These outcomes establish neither that the prize alone caused aviation’s expansion nor that the benefits outweighed the costs imposed across all competing teams.

sections.title: What happened
sections.html:
Mixed outcomes. The specified flight was achieved and publicly celebrated. Other entrants faced catastrophic losses. These outcomes establish neither that the prize alone caused aviation’s expansion nor that the benefits outweighed the costs imposed across all competing teams.

  • With underwriting from St. Louis businessmen, Lindbergh completed the flight in May 1927 and won the $25,000 award. Today in History: June 11, Lindbergh Honored
  • Charles Nungesser disappeared while attempting to win the Orteig Prize. “Knight of Death” Airplane Insignia
  • After his flight, Lindbergh became an influential spokesman for the emerging aviation industry. Today in History: June 11, Lindbergh Honored

sections.title: What might explain it
sections.html:
Plausible
