The prize’s legible route and public recognition may have helped a pilot mobilize backers. Today in History: June 11, Lindbergh Honored

Alternative explanation: Aircraft improvements, personal ambition, national rivalry, and commercial aviation opportunities also supplied powerful reasons to attempt the flight.

Supported in case

A winner-focused narrative can obscure the portfolio of risk taken by unsuccessful entrants. “Knight of Death” Airplane Insignia Today in History: June 11, Lindbergh Honored

Alternative explanation: Danger was already characteristic of frontier aviation; documenting a loss does not show that the prize increased risk beyond the relevant baseline.

sections.title: Questions to take into practice
sections.html:
• Assess entrant losses and near misses alongside the winner’s achievement.
  • Distinguish the prize payment from the up-front patronage that makes an attempt feasible.

sections.title: What remains uncertain
sections.html: • The winner’s achievement does not reveal the total spending, losses or abandoned work across all entrants. Aviation was also advancing for other reasons, making the prize’s contribution to subsequent growth difficult to separate.

title: Nupedia and Wikipedia: opening participation, then managing it
question: What changes when contributors can improve a draft immediately rather than await permission?
summary: Nupedia required articles to pass an expert review workflow; Wikipedia let contributors edit immediately. But the contrast was not simply bureaucracy versus freedom. Nupedia also lacked sustained organizing support, while the growing Wikipedia developed quality controls that made it harder for newcomers to stay. Opening the door and keeping useful participation possible became different problems.
outcome_summary: Wikipedia achieved extensive collaborative production while Nupedia faded. Later analysis associated Wikipedia’s restrictive quality controls with declining newcomer retention. Rapid contribution and reliable review had to coexist, and rules introduced to protect the encyclopedia could also discourage its future editors.

sections.title: What happened
sections.html:
Mixed outcomes. Wikipedia achieved extensive collaborative production while Nupedia faded. Later analysis associated Wikipedia’s restrictive quality controls with declining newcomer retention. Rapid contribution and reliable review had to coexist, and rules introduced to protect the encyclopedia could also discourage its future editors.

  • Sanger describes Nupedia’s seven-step process as slow, but also attributes its decline to neglect and insufficient support for paid organizing. The Early History of Nupedia and Wikipedia: A Memoir
  • His history describes attempts to simplify Nupedia while organizational attention shifted toward Wikipedia. The Early History of Nupedia and Wikipedia: A Memoir
  • Halfaker and colleagues connect Wikipedia’s newcomer-retention decline with restrictive quality controls, automated rejection, and resistance to newcomers’ proposed rule changes. The Rise and Decline of an Open Collaboration System

sections.title: What might explain it
sections.html:
Plausible

Immediate editing may increase the number of small contributions people are willing to attempt. The Early History of Nupedia and Wikipedia: A Memoir

Alternative explanation: Search visibility, recruitment, and the distribution of organizer attention also changed; the projects were not experimentally matched.

Supported in case

Controls introduced to preserve quality may inadvertently screen out future committed contributors. The Rise and Decline of an Open Collaboration System

Alternative explanation: Changes in who arrived or in the remaining editing opportunities could also influence retention; not every rejected edit represents lost valuable participation.

sections.title: Understanding the outcome
sections.html:
Open-collaboration newcomer retention, Halfaker and colleagues

Filtering contributions can protect the encyclopedia while making it harder to replenish the community that maintains it. The Rise and Decline of an Open Collaboration System

Its historical Wikipedia mechanisms are not proof that every moderation system reduces useful participation.

sections.title: Questions to take into practice
sections.html:
• Measure how often promising newcomers return after their first correction.
  • Budget for organizing and review instead of treating an editable website as a self-running institution.

sections.title: What remains uncertain
sections.html: • Sanger’s retrospective account combines a founder’s experience with disputed questions of credit and responsibility. The two projects differed in organizing support and attention as well as workflow, so their trajectories cannot isolate the effect of immediate editing.

title: Python: replacing a founder’s final say
question: Can a project replace personal authority without replacing its whole working community?
summary: After conflict over a language proposal, Guido van Rossum withdrew as Python’s final decision-maker and declined to appoint a successor. Core developers then selected a steering-council model and elected its first members. The transition changed the authority structure while retaining existing contributors, technical work, and even the founder’s participation in a different role.
outcome_summary: Core developers adopted a successor decision structure and elected its first council. Authority moved from one final decision-maker to an elected body, while the electorate remained the core developer community rather than every Python user.

sections.title: What happened
sections.html:
Bounded success. Core developers adopted a successor decision structure and elected its first council. Authority moved from one final decision-maker to an elected body, while the electorate remained the core developer community rather than every Python user.

  • Van Rossum’s resignation said he would leave the decision process, remain available as a core developer, and not choose a successor. Transfer of power
  • The adopted proposal provided a five-member council, core-team voting and safeguards against one employer dominating the council. PEP 8016: The Steering Council Model
  • The first election drew 69 ballots from 96 eligible voters and elected five members, including van Rossum. PEP 8100: January 2019 Steering Council election

sections.title: What might explain it
sections.html:
Plausible

An established contributor community may be able to redistribute final authority while preserving routine production. Transfer of power PEP 8100: January 2019 Steering Council election

Alternative explanation: Continuity may depend more on pre-existing maintainers and mature technical processes than on the council design.

Plausible

Keeping the founder involved without exclusive final authority may preserve knowledge while reducing dependence on one person. Transfer of power PEP 8100: January 2019 Steering Council election

Alternative explanation: Informal influence might remain concentrated even after formal powers are redistributed; election results do not measure actual deliberative influence.

sections.title: Questions to take into practice
sections.html:
• Identify which decisions truly depend on the founder before redesigning every role.
  • Specify electorate, replacement procedures, and employer conflicts before a vacancy becomes urgent.

sections.title: What remains uncertain
sections.html: • The transition settled who formally held final authority. How far informal influence changed, and whether contributors found later decisions better or more satisfactory, require attention to the council’s subsequent practice.

title: Heartbleed: widely used does not mean adequately maintained
question: Who supplies maintenance and incident response for infrastructure everyone depends on?
summary: Heartbleed exposed a serious vulnerability in the widely used OpenSSL library. The response required more than a public patch: operators needed to identify exposure and act. Industry subsequently organized pooled support for important open-source projects. The case connects maintenance funding, distributed responsibility, and the practical work of getting a repair adopted.
outcome_summary: The vulnerability produced widespread exposure, followed by patching and new support arrangements. Direct notification improved patching among contacted operators. Pooled funding committed support for developers and an audit, while maintaining the code and getting repairs deployed remained continuing responsibilities.

sections.title: What happened
sections.html:
Mixed outcomes. The vulnerability produced widespread exposure, followed by patching and new support arrangements. Direct notification improved patching among contacted operators. Pooled funding committed support for developers and an audit, while maintaining the code and getting repairs deployed remained continuing responsibilities.

  • The vulnerability exposed protected memory, and affected operators varied substantially in how quickly they patched after disclosure. The Matter of Heartbleed
  • Operators receiving direct notifications patched more often in a staged notification experiment. The Matter of Heartbleed
  • The Linux Foundation announced support for two full-time OpenSSL developers and an external security audit through the Core Infrastructure Initiative. Core Infrastructure Initiative Announces First Projects to Receive Support

sections.title: What might explain it
sections.html:
Supported in case

Direct notification can overcome some operational inattention after a widely publicized vulnerability. The Matter of Heartbleed

Alternative explanation: The effect could depend on identifying reachable administrators; unreachable or abandoned services may require a different response.

Plausible

Users who benefit from shared code may underinvest in collective maintenance until a crisis makes dependencies visible. Core Infrastructure Initiative Announces First Projects to Receive Support The Matter of Heartbleed

Alternative explanation: This incident could also reflect difficult code review and deployment coordination that additional funding alone would not solve.

sections.title: Understanding the outcome
sections.html:
Collective-action/free-rider problem in shared infrastructure

Many beneficiaries and concentrated maintenance work make financing responsibility a useful question. Core Infrastructure Initiative Announces First Projects to Receive Support

The case does not compare open and proprietary software security or establish that unpaid work caused this specific bug.

sections.title: Questions to take into practice
sections.html:
• Inventory critical dependencies and identify who maintains them before a crisis.
  • Treat publication of a fix and verified downstream adoption as different milestones.

sections.title: What remains uncertain
sections.html: • Support commitments for developers and audits did not themselves show whether long-term security improved. Successful notification addressed adoption of a repair, leaving open how to prevent similar defects during development.

title: Debian and Devuan: a vote can settle a rule without settling a dispute
question: What happens when a formal decision leaves participants with incompatible visions?
summary: Debian debated whether packages should be required to support alternative initialization systems. Its formal resolution process produced a decision, but dissenting developers and administrators still regarded the project’s direction as unacceptable. They announced Devuan, a derivative intended to avoid systemd dependencies. Open licensing made exit with reusable code possible alongside continued disagreement.
outcome_summary: Debian reached a binding decision, and dissenters began a separate project. A procedure allowed the existing project to proceed without reconciling its participants’ competing priorities; open licensing gave those leaving a starting point for their own work.

sections.title: What happened
sections.html:
Mixed outcomes. Debian reached a binding decision, and dissenters began a separate project. A procedure allowed the existing project to proceed without reconciling its participants’ competing priorities; open licensing gave those leaving a starting point for their own work.

  • “General Resolution is not required” defeated every other option in the 2014 preference vote. General Resolution: init system coupling
  • The rejected proposals concerned package dependencies and support obligations, a different question from the earlier choice of a default initialization system. General Resolution: init system coupling
  • Devuan’s founders described their fork as a response to disagreements about governance and mission as well as technical design. Announcement of the Debian Fork

sections.title: What might explain it
sections.html:
Supported in case

A formal vote may preserve a project’s ability to proceed without making minority participants accept its priorities. General Resolution: init system coupling Announcement of the Debian Fork

Alternative explanation: The departure might have happened even without this vote because technical commitments had already diverged.

Plausible

Forkability may convert an otherwise blocked internal dispute into parallel experimentation. Announcement of the Debian Fork

Alternative explanation: Parallel projects may instead duplicate scarce maintenance work and retain dependencies on the upstream community they leave.

sections.title: Questions to take into practice
sections.html:
• Ask whether a decision procedure promises a binding decision or genuine convergence; those are different outcomes.
  • Before proposing a fork, identify the maintainers, infrastructure, and continuing upstream dependencies it would need.

sections.title: What remains uncertain
sections.html: • Devuan’s founders presented their own account of the dispute, which does not establish how representative their grievances were across Debian. The fork’s longer-term value also depends on adoption, quality and the extra maintenance required.

title: Linux and Android: the cost of freedom to diverge
question: How can a shared codebase support variation without making repairs prohibitively expensive?
period: Pre-GKI Android kernels through Android 12-era restructuring
summary: Linux integrates contributions through subsystem maintainers, while downstream organizations can adapt the code for particular products. Android’s device-specific kernels illustrate the maintenance cost of that variation. Google’s Generic Kernel Image project sought to reunify the core while moving vendor-specific support into modules, changing the coordination boundary instead of eliminating all specialization.
outcome_summary: Android introduced a shared kernel and module boundary in response to the difficulty of updating divergent device kernels. The architecture changed where customization could occur. Its practical security benefit still depends on manufacturers delivering repairs through to users’ devices.

sections.title: What happened
sections.html:
Mixed outcomes. Android introduced a shared kernel and module boundary in response to the difficulty of updating divergent device kernels. The architecture changed where customization could occur. Its practical security benefit still depends on manufacturers delivering repairs through to users’ devices.

  • Contributions pass through a chain of subsystem maintainers before integration into Linux’s mainline repository. How the development process works
  • Android’s account identifies custom device kernels as a source of difficult security backports, delayed upgrades, and costly upstream contribution. Generic Kernel Image project
  • GKI moves hardware-specific support into modules around a common kernel and stable module interface, with requirements applying to relevant Android 12 launches. Generic Kernel Image project

sections.title: What might explain it
sections.html:
Plausible

Shared integration boundaries may reduce duplicated adaptation work without removing product-specific variation. Generic Kernel Image project How the development process works

Alternative explanation: Benefits may depend on central platform enforcement and vendor resources rather than modularity alone.

Plausible

Permission to fork is valuable only when participants can sustain the integration work it creates. Generic Kernel Image project

Alternative explanation: Some divergence is necessary for unsupported hardware or independent priorities; convergence could sacrifice useful autonomy.

sections.title: Questions to take into practice
sections.html:
• Estimate the lifetime cost of carrying a private branch, not just the cost of making the initial modification.
  • Design explicit paths for downstream improvements and repairs to return to the shared core.

sections.title: What remains uncertain
sections.html: • Google’s diagnosis explains the intended benefit of GKI. Measuring its realized effect requires following update delivery across manufacturers, including differences in their resources and implementation. The Linux maintainer hierarchy and Android’s downstream requirements exercise authority at different points in that process.

title: Zano: a funded campaign is not a delivered product
question: What does a crowd validate when it backs an ambitious hardware demonstration?
summary: Zano’s small-drone campaign raised far more than its target while promising polished autonomous behavior. The company later pursued liquidation and most backers received nothing. A Kickstarter-commissioned investigation found gaps between the promotional demonstration, technical readiness and delivery capacity. Money had arrived before the team could reliably deliver what it had sold.
outcome_summary: The campaign mobilized substantial money but failed to deliver the promised product to most backers. Investigation after the collapse helped explain what went wrong, without restoring the missing drones or funds.

sections.title: What happened
sections.html:
Failure on the stated objective. The campaign mobilized substantial money but failed to deliver the promised product to most backers. Investigation after the collapse helped explain what went wrong, without restoring the missing drones or funds.

  • The campaign set a £125,000 target and made strong promotional claims about readiness. According to Harris’s investigation, only four Kickstarter backers ultimately received drones. How Zano Raised Millions on Kickstarter and Left Most Backers with Nothing
  • Delivered units failed to perform as the promotional video suggested. Kickstarter backers were distinct from a separate group of pre-order customers. How Zano Raised Millions on Kickstarter and Left Most Backers with Nothing
  • Torquing announced that it would pursue creditors’ voluntary liquidation. BBC: Zano mini-drone project shut down by Torquing

sections.title: What might explain it
sections.html:
Supported in case

A compelling demonstration may attract funding without validating repeatable product performance or manufacturing readiness. How Zano Raised Millions on Kickstarter and Left Most Backers with Nothing

Alternative explanation: Backers may knowingly accept prototype risk; the key failure could instead be inaccurate representations about how much remained unfinished.

Plausible

Rapidly exceeding a campaign target may increase execution demands faster than organizational capability. How Zano Raised Millions on Kickstarter and Left Most Backers with Nothing BBC: Zano mini-drone project shut down by Torquing

Alternative explanation: The original technical plan may already have been infeasible; additional demand need not be the primary cause of collapse.

sections.title: Questions to take into practice
sections.html:
• Ask for repeatable demonstrations and a manufacturing plan separately from attractive promotional footage.
  • State what platform endorsement and funding milestones do and do not verify.

sections.title: What remains uncertain
sections.html: • Kickstarter paid for the main investigation, although the reporter said the platform could not edit it. Interviews and contemporary reporting clarify the delivery failure but leave the full financial allocation less certain.

title: Fagor: a cooperative can fail while its network still protects people
question: Does institutional resilience mean saving every firm, or helping people survive a firm’s failure?
location: Basque Country, Spain; subsidiaries in France and Poland
summary: Fagor Electrodomésticos went bankrupt inside the Mondragon cooperative network. Preserving the enterprise and protecting its members proved to be different tasks. Relocation, retraining and support offered displaced workers other paths, but some placements were insecure and receiving cooperatives resisted taking workers permanently. Solidarity depended on agreements across organizations with their own pressures.
outcome_summary: Fagor failed, while the network helped absorb some consequences through relocation and support. Those protections depended on receiving cooperatives and workers’ circumstances; they did not erase the losses or reach everyone equally.

sections.title: What happened
sections.html:
Mixed outcomes. Fagor failed, while the network helped absorb some consequences through relocation and support. Those protections depended on receiving cooperatives and workers’ circumstances; they did not erase the losses or reach everyone equally.

  • Fagor went bankrupt in November 2013 after international expansion and restructuring across its parent plants and European subsidiaries. What Do Mondragon Coopitalist Multinationals Look Like? The Rise and Fall of Fagor
  • Relocation and retraining offered displaced workers routes into other cooperatives, but some workers objected to temporary placements and receiving cooperatives resisted making them permanent. Intercooperation, flexicurity and their impact on workers: The case of Fagor Electrodomésticos
  • Mondragon and Lagun Aro could not simply impose relocations on other cooperatives. Intercooperation, flexicurity and their impact on workers: The case of Fagor Electrodomésticos

sections.title: What might explain it
sections.html:
Plausible

Federated institutions may protect members against enterprise-specific failure more effectively than an isolated cooperative could. Intercooperation, flexicurity and their impact on workers: The case of Fagor Electrodomésticos

Alternative explanation: A conventional group with strong employment insurance and regional support might provide similar protection; ownership is not the only mechanism.

Supported in case

Solidarity becomes harder when helping displaced insiders competes with local hiring and another cooperative’s flexibility. Intercooperation, flexicurity and their impact on workers: The case of Fagor Electrodomésticos

Alternative explanation: Skills mismatch, market weakness, and existing workforce commitments can explain reluctance without assuming selfishness or ideological collapse.

sections.title: Understanding the outcome
sections.html:
Flexicurity in cooperative intercooperation

Employment security depended partly on workers moving between cooperatives, linking protection from unemployment to flexibility about where and how they worked. Intercooperation, flexicurity and their impact on workers: The case of Fagor Electrodomésticos

Interview evidence does not establish how a comparable conventional network would have performed.

sections.title: Questions to take into practice
sections.html:
• Define whether a mutual-support promise protects jobs, income, membership, or a particular workplace.
  • Ask who is excluded from protection when enterprises employ nonmembers or operate foreign subsidiaries.

sections.title: What remains uncertain
sections.html: • Workers’ accounts reveal conflicting experiences of relocation without establishing how widespread satisfaction or dissatisfaction was. Protection for cooperative members also needs to be distinguished from the experience of nonmembers and employees in foreign subsidiaries.

title: Grameen II: rewriting the rules did not instantly change the meetings
question: What happens when frontline habits preserve a practice that a formal reform tries to remove?
summary: Grameen II introduced more flexible loan arrangements while retaining borrower groups and regular meetings. Its rules rejected making members repay another borrower’s debt. Yet early fieldwork found meeting practices that pressured members to cover shortfalls. Changing the written terms did not immediately change how staff secured repayment or how borrowers experienced responsibility.
outcome_summary: The redesigned system offered repayment flexibility, but implementation was uneven. Formal individual responsibility coexisted with collective pressure in observed branches, making staff behavior crucial to what the new rules meant for borrowers.

sections.title: What happened
sections.html:
Mixed outcomes. The redesigned system offered repayment flexibility, but implementation was uneven. Formal individual responsibility coexisted with collective pressure in observed branches, making staff behavior crucial to what the new rules meant for borrowers.

  • Under the Grameen II design, borrowers encountering difficulty could renegotiate a flexible loan with a revised repayment schedule. Guidelines for Establishing and Operating Grameen-style Microcredit Programs, Annex 2.1
  • Despite the explicit no-joint-liability rule, fieldworkers observed pressure on members to cover other borrowers’ repayments. Grameen II at the end of 2003: A grounded view
  • In observed meetings, staff delayed closing or providing other services until dues were covered; some staff also resisted offering flexible loans. Grameen II at the end of 2003: A grounded view

sections.title: What might explain it
sections.html:
Supported in case

Established routines may survive formal reform when staff believe flexibility threatens repayment discipline. Grameen II at the end of 2003: A grounded view

Alternative explanation: Some staff behavior may instead reflect local repayment conditions or incentives not adequately captured in the report.

Participant explanation

Individual renegotiation could reduce the burden placed on other group members without eliminating mutual information and support. Guidelines for Establishing and Operating Grameen-style Microcredit Programs, Annex 2.1

Alternative explanation: Flexibility may be inaccessible in practice, or merely extend indebtedness; stated intentions do not establish borrower welfare improvements.

sections.title: Questions to take into practice
sections.html:
• Observe meetings and exception handling rather than inferring practice from a rulebook.
  • Ask whether frontline incentives and training support the discretion a reform officially permits.

sections.title: What remains uncertain
sections.html: • The observed meetings cover a limited early implementation sample. They leave open how widely these practices persisted as the reform developed, and whether accessible renegotiation improved borrowers’ welfare.

title: Hyderabad microcredit: more borrowing, no general transformation
question: Does expanded access to small business credit produce the broader changes its advocates expect?
summary: Spandana expanded group-lending services into randomly selected Hyderabad neighborhoods, allowing researchers to compare earlier access with later access. Borrowing and some business investment increased. But greater access did not produce significant average improvements in several wider measures of household welfare: the step from more credit to a transformed livelihood was far from automatic.
outcome_summary: Earlier access changed borrowing and some economic choices without significant average improvements in consumption, health, education, or the measured women’s-empowerment outcomes. A six-study synthesis found similarly modest rather than transformative effects across varied settings, while leaving room for heterogeneous benefits and costs.

sections.title: What happened
sections.html:
Mixed outcomes. Earlier access changed borrowing and some economic choices without significant average improvements in consumption, health, education, or the measured women’s-empowerment outcomes. A six-study synthesis found similarly modest rather than transformative effects across varied settings, while leaving room for heterogeneous benefits and costs.

  • The study randomized 52 of 104 neighborhoods to earlier Spandana access; actual borrowing increased rather than becoming universal. The Miracle of Microfinance? Evidence from a Randomized Evaluation
  • Researchers report increased investment and profits among existing businesses, but no significant average gain in consumption or several broader social outcomes. The Miracle of Microfinance? Evidence from a Randomized Evaluation
  • Across six randomized evaluations in varied settings, average effects were modest rather than the broad transformations often attributed to microcredit. Six Randomized Evaluations of Microcredit: Introduction and Further Steps

sections.title: What might explain it
sections.html:
Plausible

Credit can relax a constraint for some existing entrepreneurs without making most households successful new business owners. The Miracle of Microfinance? Evidence from a Randomized Evaluation Six Randomized Evaluations of Microcredit: Introduction and Further Steps

Alternative explanation: Demand, skills, risk, and repayment obligations may matter more than access to capital for many households.

Supported in case

Large universal poverty-reduction expectations were not supported by the outcomes and horizons evaluated here. The Miracle of Microfinance? Evidence from a Randomized Evaluation Six Randomized Evaluations of Microcredit: Introduction and Further Steps

Alternative explanation: Longer-run effects or concentrated gains for particular borrowers may be obscured by average estimates and later control-group access.

sections.title: Understanding the outcome
sections.html:
Credit constraints and heterogeneous returns to microenterprise investment

Separates expanded availability from guaranteed take-up or uniform entrepreneurial returns. The Miracle of Microfinance? Evidence from a Randomized Evaluation Six Randomized Evaluations of Microcredit: Introduction and Further Steps

Assignment estimates concern access under these conditions, not the effect of every loan or the quality of Grameen’s organizational model.

sections.title: Questions to take into practice
sections.html:
• Name the welfare outcome and time horizon before treating repayment or borrower counts as success.
  • Compare effects for different participants without turning subgroup anecdotes into universal promises.

sections.title: What remains uncertain
sections.html: • The synthesis includes this trial and is not a second independent replication of Hyderabad. Later control access changes the interpretation of follow-up differences. Migration exclusions and imperfect take-up narrow generalization.

title: Haifa daycare fines: paying to be late?
question: Can a penalty change what people think they are allowed to do?
period: January–June 1998 field study; published 2000; later laboratory mechanism study
summary: Researchers introduced a small late-pickup fine at six of ten daycare centers. Lateness increased instead of falling and remained elevated during the short period after removal. A charge intended to discourage delay may have made extra care feel like something parents could buy. The behavior changed clearly; the parents’ interpretation is harder to establish.
outcome_summary: The fine failed to reduce lateness in these centers. A later laboratory experiment explored how penalties and payment recipients could change behavior, but used a different task and could not establish what the daycare parents had believed.

sections.title: What happened
sections.html:
Failure on the stated objective. The fine failed to reduce lateness in these centers. A later laboratory experiment explored how penalties and payment recipients could change behavior, but used a different task and could not establish what the daycare parents had believed.

  • The field study observed ten centers for twenty weeks and randomly selected six for a fine introduced after the initial observation period. A Fine Is a Price
  • The fine was NIS 10 for a qualifying late pickup; recorded lateness increased and did not return to baseline during four weeks after withdrawal. A Fine Is a Price
  • A later real-effort experiment varied penalties and who received payment, finding different responses by social-value orientation rather than a uniform average crowding-out effect. Testing a Fine Is a Price in the Lab

sections.title: What might explain it
sections.html:
Plausible

Parents may have interpreted the fine as a defined price for extra care instead of a signal that lateness was unacceptable. A Fine Is a Price Testing a Fine Is a Price in the Lab

Alternative explanation: A small specified penalty could instead reduce uncertainty about previously feared consequences; these explanations overlap but are not identical.

Supported in case

The meaning and recipient of payment can alter its effect alongside its monetary size. Testing a Fine Is a Price in the Lab

Alternative explanation: The laboratory uses contract performance, not parents and caregivers; selection and subgroup classification constrain transfer to everyday sanctions.

sections.title: Understanding the outcome
sections.html:
Fine-is-a-price framing and motivational crowding

Distinguishes the observed increase in lateness from a proposed change in the perceived social contract. A Fine Is a Price Testing a Fine Is a Price in the Lab

Neither study establishes that substantial fines, all cultural settings, or all participants respond the same way.

sections.title: Questions to take into practice
sections.html:
• Ask what a new charge communicates about permission, obligation, and who bears the harm.
  • Measure behavior after removing an incentive rather than assuming the previous norm returns immediately.

sections.title: What remains uncertain
sections.html: • The field sample was small and two initially observed centers were excluded for incomplete records. Post-removal observation was brief. The later laboratory study tests a related mechanism, not a direct daycare replication.

title: Blood donation incentives: one crowding-out story is not a universal law
question: When do payments change participation, and when do they merely move it elsewhere?
period: Swedish experiment published 2008; US study published 2012
summary: A Swedish experiment offered prospective blood donors no payment, a small payment, or payment with a charity option. The negative effect appeared among women, while differences across all participants were not statistically significant. US blood-drive research later found increased donations with incentives, partly offset by movement between drives. Payments changed participation differently across these settings and measures.
outcome_summary: The Swedish pooled differences were not statistically significant; the authors reported crowding out among women and reversal with the charity option. US evidence found increased donations at incentivized drives, partly offset by movement from neighboring drives. Context and the measured outcome change the conclusion.

sections.title: What happened
sections.html:
Mixed outcomes. The Swedish pooled differences were not statistically significant; the authors reported crowding out among women and reversal with the charity option. US evidence found increased donations at incentivized drives, partly offset by movement from neighboring drives. Context and the measured outcome change the conclusion.

  • Mellström and Johannesson report pooled participation of 43%, 33%, and 44% across treatments, with differences not statistically significant; the women’s subgroup showed a significant payment decline. Crowding Out in Blood Donation: Was Titmuss Right?
  • Their intervention concerned agreeing to become a donor, not a demonstrated long-term change in safe blood supply. Crowding Out in Blood Donation: Was Titmuss Right?
  • In US blood-drive data and a field experiment, incentives increased donations at participating drives, but some of that gain came from donors switching away from neighboring drives. Will There Be Blood? Incentives and Displacement Effects in Pro-social Behavior

sections.title: What might explain it
sections.html:
Plausible

A payment may alter the social meaning of an altruistic action differently for different participants. Crowding Out in Blood Donation: Was Titmuss Right?

Alternative explanation: Small subgroups, pre-existing preferences, or context-specific interpretations could explain heterogeneity without implying a stable gender rule.

Supported in case

A local participation increase can overstate a system-wide increase when people switch locations. Will There Be Blood? Incentives and Displacement Effects in Pro-social Behavior

Alternative explanation: Some additional attendance may represent genuinely new or better-timed donations; displacement need not eliminate all benefit.

sections.title: Understanding the outcome
sections.html:
Motivational crowding and displacement

Separates reduced willingness in one setting from substitution and increased observed donations elsewhere. Crowding Out in Blood Donation: Was Titmuss Right? Will There Be Blood? Incentives and Displacement Effects in Pro-social Behavior

Cash versus other incentives, prospective versus established donors, and outcome definitions prevent treating these as identical interventions.

sections.title: Questions to take into practice
sections.html:
• Distinguish willingness, attendance, completed donation, and total supply before comparing studies.
  • Track neighboring venues and later participation when evaluating a local incentive.

sections.title: What remains uncertain
sections.html: • Agreement to become a donor, completed donations and sustained safe blood supply are different outcomes. Neither a small subgroup’s response nor an increase at selected drives settles the long-term effect of a payment policy on the whole supply system.

title: Cocoon Projects: contribution-weighted governance with LiquidO
question: Can open participation coexist with authority weighted by assessed contribution?
period: Model documented in 2013; external mapping in 2016–2017
summary: Stelio Verzera describes LiquidO as Cocoon Projects’ operating model: people pull collectively prioritized work from a shared board, assess contributions after delivery, and receive credits convertible into compensation. Some consequential votes are weighted by earned credits. It is therefore a specific combination of open participation and differentiated influence, rather than equal-vote democracy or an absence of structure.
outcome_summary: LiquidO combined open participation with contribution-weighted compensation and voting inside a privately owned company. Verzera reported close agreement between self-assessment and peer assessments, but agreement alone cannot show whether less visible work received fair credit or whether newcomers could gain influence.

sections.title: What happened
sections.html:
Outcome evidence uncertain. LiquidO combined open participation with contribution-weighted compensation and voting inside a privately owned company. Verzera reported close agreement between self-assessment and peer assessments, but agreement alone cannot show whether less visible work received fair credit or whether newcomers could gain influence.

  • The 2013 LiquidO design combined time-boxed voting, work-in-progress limits, voluntary task uptake, and peer evaluation of completed contributions. Liquid organizations: building the next evolutionary stage of anti-fragility
  • Credits determine compensation and, for decisions deemed important, differentiated voting weight. The founder reports assessment discrepancies below 10%, without publishing the underlying dataset. Liquid organizations: building the next evolutionary stage of anti-fragility
  • Cocoon remained privately owned while opening parts of its governance to participants. Participation in decisions did not itself give contributors ownership rights. Positive Platforms Identity: Italian ecosystem mapping

sections.title: What might explain it
sections.html:
Participant explanation

Visible contribution records could make informal influence discussable and reward neglected organizational work. Liquid organizations: building the next evolutionary stage of anti-fragility

Alternative explanation: A closely selected professional group and repeated relationships may explain cooperative behavior independently of the credit system.

Plausible

Accumulated credits could also reinforce incumbents’ influence rather than keep authority responsive to current expertise. Liquid organizations: building the next evolutionary stage of anti-fragility

Alternative explanation: Credit expiry or decision rules tied to relevant expertise could limit this effect. Whether those safeguards operated in LiquidO remains unclear.

sections.title: Understanding the outcome
sections.html:
Stigmergic coordination

The shared board provides visible traces that guide subsequent work without assigning every task centrally. Liquid organizations: building the next evolutionary stage of anti-fragility

A shared task board can decentralize task choice while leaving evaluation, conflict resolution, and ownership concentrated.

sections.title: Questions to take into practice
sections.html:
• Which decisions are open to everyone, and which give more weight to past contributors?
  • How are disputed assessments, essential invisible work, and newcomers’ influence handled?

sections.title: What remains uncertain
sections.html:
• How did voting weight change as credits accumulated, and how much influence could a newcomer acquire?
  • The durability of the arrangement, the treatment of departures, and the experience of people dissatisfied with their assessments remain unclear.

title: Enspiral: support networks can develop their own forms of pressure
question: What replaces managerial control when work, friendship, and care overlap?
period: Network founded around 2010; an 18-month field study published in 2021
location: Wellington, New Zealand, with international participants
summary: Enspiral connects people and ventures pursuing socially meaningful work through shared relationships, support practices, and organizational infrastructure. It is a network containing distinct ventures, not one uniformly managed company. Formal agreements coexist with editable guides, while work, friendship, personal growth, and belonging overlap in everyday participation.
outcome_summary: During an 18-month field study, participants experienced practical generosity and early opportunities to contribute, alongside exhaustion, pressure to disclose personal feelings, and strained boundaries. Support could open doors while expectations of openness made participation demanding. These experiences concern particular people and occasions, not every member or the network today.

sections.title: What happened
sections.html:
Mixed outcomes. During an 18-month field study, participants experienced practical generosity and early opportunities to contribute, alongside exhaustion, pressure to disclose personal feelings, and strained boundaries. Support could open doors while expectations of openness made participation demanding. These experiences concern particular people and occasions, not every member or the network today.

  • Enspiral distinguishes agreements requiring formal change from guides contributors can edit, and combines nodes and working groups with a foundation holding formal roles. Enspiral Handbook: Introduction and Structure
  • The network included roughly 200–350 participants during the field-study period, spanning relationships beyond any one venture. Affective Control in New Collaborative Work: Communal Fantasies of Purpose, Growth and Belonging
  • Check-ins gave participants opportunities to share personal circumstances. Some also described excessive disclosure, overextended care, and discomfort about what participation seemed to require. Affective Control in New Collaborative Work: Communal Fantasies of Purpose, Growth and Belonging

sections.title: What might explain it
sections.html:
Supported in case

Relational openness can become an informal admission test for being trusted with important work. Affective Control in New Collaborative Work: Communal Fantasies of Purpose, Growth and Belonging

Alternative explanation: Some discomfort may reflect particular meetings or facilitator choices rather than an unavoidable feature of network organizing.

Plausible

Clearer boundaries and named support responsibilities might preserve care without leaving a few people feeling responsible for everyone. Affective Control in New Collaborative Work: Communal Fantasies of Purpose, Growth and Belonging Enspiral Handbook: Introduction and Structure

Alternative explanation: Resource scarcity and uneven availability may still concentrate the work even when responsibilities are documented.

sections.title: Understanding the outcome
sections.html:
Affective control in collaborative work

Desires for purpose, growth, and belonging can generate commitment and pressure without a conventional boss. The term “affective control” draws attention to how those desires influence participation. Affective Control in New Collaborative Work: Communal Fantasies of Purpose, Growth and Belonging

The same check-in may feel supportive to one person and intrusive to another; meeting design and relationships affect how pressure develops.

sections.title: Questions to take into practice
sections.html:
• Can someone decline emotional disclosure and remain a trusted participant?
  • Who performs care and coordination, and what happens when those people stop?
  • Separate the network’s support function from the governance and employment rules of individual ventures.

sections.title: What remains uncertain
sections.html:
• How do people who leave Enspiral experience these expectations, and which participants carry the greatest care burden?
  • The fieldwork and later handbook describe different periods; changes in formal rules may also have changed everyday experiences.

title: Enspiral’s Cobudget: open proposals still need timing and strategy
question: Why can a transparent participatory budget leave money idle or miss shared priorities?
location: Enspiral network, New Zealand and distributed
summary: Enspiral developed collaborative funding after a small support crew became overwhelmed by coordination. Members could propose funding buckets, while contributors allocated discretionary money after core costs. Later experience revealed that continuous proposal flows, scattered attention, and idle balances did not automatically produce a coherent shared budget, prompting facilitated rounds and strategic conversations.
outcome_summary: Early organizers reported broader participation and lower coordination costs. Later, steward Francesca Pick encountered low-priority spending, timing advantages, and unused allocations. She judged the projects more strategic after three facilitated rounds, although that judgment leaves open whether the funded work produced better long-term results.

sections.title: What happened
sections.html:
Mixed outcomes. Early organizers reported broader participation and lower coordination costs. Later, steward Francesca Pick encountered low-priority spending, timing advantages, and unused allocations. She judged the projects more strategic after three facilitated rounds, although that judgment leaves open whether the funded work produced better long-term results.

  • The 2014 design reserved core expenses before discretionary allocation; anyone could propose a bucket, while allocation rights initially followed financial contributions. Collaborative Funding: dissolve authority, empower everyone, and crowdsource a smarter, transparent budget
  • During continuous funding, money remained unused in some accounts, proposals were difficult to compare, and attention was scattered across the network. Sharing power by sharing money: the evolution of collaborative funding in Enspiral
  • Time-boxed rounds added strategic discussion and a facilitator. Pick reported three rounds allocating about US$40,000; her favorable judgment concerned the strategic quality of the selected projects. Sharing power by sharing money: the evolution of collaborative funding in Enspiral

sections.title: What might explain it
sections.html:
Participant explanation

Synchronized rounds may improve comparison by placing competing proposals in view at the same time. Sharing power by sharing money: the evolution of collaborative funding in Enspiral

Alternative explanation: Different proposers, funding levels, or greater organizer experience could also account for the changed portfolio.

Plausible

Giving every contributor control over an allocation can spread power while still leaving coordination work concentrated. Collaborative Funding: dissolve authority, empower everyone, and crowdsource a smarter, transparent budget Sharing power by sharing money: the evolution of collaborative funding in Enspiral

Alternative explanation: A network with stable priorities and experienced participants may require less facilitation than this transition did.

sections.title: Questions to take into practice
sections.html:
• Distinguish permission to propose from rights to allocate money.
  • Can members compare alternatives before committing their allocations?
  • Provide a separate route for urgent proposals that cannot wait for a round.

sections.title: What remains uncertain
sections.html:
• Did the projects funded through facilitated rounds produce more lasting value than those selected through continuous allocation?
  • How did unequal allocation rights and members who rarely participated affect the resulting budget?

title: Microsolidarity practice programs: from strangers to small support groups
question: Can a short program help strangers form support groups that continue meeting?
summary: Richard D. Bartlett’s microsolidarity proposal names a small recurring support group a crew and a wider environment for forming crews a congregation. Drawing partly on Enspiral experience, Bartlett and Nati Lombardo ran online practice programs that moved participants through paired encounters, small-group support, and reflection. The aim was to give people experience of offering and receiving support, with a path toward continuing relationships.
outcome_summary: The organizers ran programs in 2020–2021 and described participants experiencing connection and insight. Whether those encounters became durable support relationships remains unclear: a satisfying session and a crew that continues exchanging practical help are different achievements.

sections.title: What happened
sections.html:
Outcome evidence uncertain. The organizers ran programs in 2020–2021 and described participants experiencing connection and insight. Whether those encounters became durable support relationships remains unclear: a satisfying session and a crew that continues exchanging practical help are different achievements.

  • Crews and congregations name patterns Bartlett recognized in Enspiral and other communities, rather than a single organization with uniform membership rules. Update 2020: Three Essential Pillars for a New Mutual Aid Community
  • Programs used four weekly 90-minute sessions for about 20–30 participants, with at least two hosts and theoretical material outside the calls. How To Run a Practice Program
  • Sessions combined brief pair encounters, Troika Consulting, Case Clinic, and a retrospective, ending with feedback and consideration of subsequent actions. How To Run a Practice Program

sections.title: What might explain it
sections.html:
Participant explanation

Repeated practice across progressively larger groupings may reduce the difficulty of approaching strangers for meaningful support. How To Run a Practice Program

Alternative explanation: Self-selection, skilled hosts, or the novelty of the event may explain positive reactions more than the sequence itself.

Participant explanation

A crew’s recurring commitment may help turn retreat enthusiasm into sustained support. Update 2020: Three Essential Pillars for a New Mutual Aid Community

Alternative explanation: Existing friendships, available time, and compatible work may determine continuity regardless of the crew label.

sections.title: Understanding the outcome
sections.html:
Microsolidarity’s nested relational scales

It distinguishes personal reflection, pairs, small crews, and a larger congregation rather than assuming one group size serves every purpose. Update 2020: Three Essential Pillars for a New Mutual Aid Community

The proposed sizes organize different kinds of interaction; they are not established optimal group sizes, and the program is peer support rather than clinical care.

sections.title: Questions to take into practice
sections.html:
• A crew becomes consequential through the help exchanged after the program, not just the closeness felt during it.
  • Optional disclosure lets people seek peer support without being required to expose private experiences.
  • Hosting and follow-up require time even when the eventual relationships are voluntary.

sections.title: What remains uncertain
sections.html:
• How many crews continued meeting, what help changed hands, and why did others dissolve?
  • The experience of people who withdrew or felt uncomfortable is less visible than the organizers’ positive accounts.

title: Buurtzorg: small nursing teams with a shared backbone
question: What replaces middle management when a professional service scales?
summary: Buurtzorg organizes home nursing around small teams that coordinate patients, schedules, recruitment, and local relationships. Coaches, software, and a central office support those teams. The distinctive arrangement is not simply removing supervisors: it redistributes managerial work while retaining shared infrastructure and relying on qualified professionals delivering a locally organized service.
outcome_summary: Buurtzorg grew substantially and attracted favorable patient and staff assessments. A historical KPMG comparison found relatively low adjusted home-care costs but roughly average total healthcare costs. Lower spending within the nursing service therefore did not translate into an equivalent reduction across all care, and the contribution of team autonomy remains difficult to separate from nursing expertise and patient differences.

sections.title: What happened
sections.html:
Mixed outcomes. Buurtzorg grew substantially and attracted favorable patient and staff assessments. A historical KPMG comparison found relatively low adjusted home-care costs but roughly average total healthcare costs. Lower spending within the nursing service therefore did not translate into an equivalent reduction across all care, and the contribution of team autonomy remains difficult to separate from nursing expertise and patient differences.

  • Teams carried responsibilities normally assigned to managers, with coaches and a central office supplying support. Buurtzorg: scaling up an organization with hundreds of self-managing teams but no middle managers
  • Adjusted home-care expenditure was below the comparison average, while total healthcare expenditure was around average. Home Care by Self-Governing Nursing Teams: The Netherlands’ Buurtzorg Model
  • Qualified nurses coordinated relatively separable local services, reducing the need for every daily decision to pass through a central office. Buurtzorg: scaling up an organization with hundreds of self-managing teams but no middle managers

sections.title: What might explain it
sections.html:
Plausible

Local decision rights may reduce handoffs between the person who knows a patient and the person authorizing care. Buurtzorg: scaling up an organization with hundreds of self-managing teams but no middle managers

Alternative explanation: Professional selection, nursing skill, or continuity of staffing could account for benefits without the entire governance model.

Supported in case

Shared administrative support may be as important as team autonomy to keeping coordination manageable. Buurtzorg: scaling up an organization with hundreds of self-managing teams but no middle managers

Alternative explanation: A different service with heavy cross-team dependencies may need more centralized scheduling and integration.

sections.title: Understanding the outcome
sections.html:
Functional substitutes for hierarchy

Managerial functions still need owners when managerial positions disappear. Buurtzorg: scaling up an organization with hundreds of self-managing teams but no middle managers

Services with tightly interdependent teams may require more central integration than local home-nursing teams do.

sections.title: Questions to take into practice
sections.html:
• List the work performed by managers before deciding which positions to remove.
  • Measure total costs and patient outcomes, not just the budget line that the new team controls.

sections.title: What remains uncertain
sections.html:
• How much of the cost difference reflected the patients served, staffing continuity, or nursing expertise rather than decision rights?
  • The workload of coaches, teams that struggled, and care supplied informally by relatives may change the apparent balance of costs and benefits.

title: East London: importing self-management into an NHS organization
question: What happens when an autonomous-team model meets an existing institution?
summary: An East London community nursing pilot adapted Buurtzorg within an established NHS provider. Nurses sought more continuous relationships with patients and greater control of daily work, while the parent organization retained significant operational and financial authority. Changing the team format did not automatically transfer the surrounding permissions over staffing and spending.
outcome_summary: Participants valued continuity and accessibility but also encountered staffing difficulties and disagreement over how much autonomy nurses actually had. The evaluation included 23 interviews, only four with patients or carers, so those favorable experiences give a limited view of patient outcomes. Clinical and financial advantages over ordinary services remained unresolved.

sections.title: What happened
sections.html:
Mixed outcomes. Participants valued continuity and accessibility but also encountered staffing difficulties and disagreement over how much autonomy nurses actually had. The evaluation included 23 interviews, only four with patients or carers, so those favorable experiences give a limited view of patient outcomes. Clinical and financial advantages over ordinary services remained unresolved.

  • Patient and carer perspectives came from four interviewees within a 23-interview evaluation, limiting how widely their experiences can be generalized. Transforming community nursing services in the UK: lessons from a participatory evaluation of the implementation of a new community nursing model in East London
  • Nurses described meaningful clinical discretion but limitations on operational and budgetary autonomy; managerial interpretations differed. Transforming community nursing services in the UK: lessons from a participatory evaluation of the implementation of a new community nursing model in East London
  • Buurtzorg-inspired teams in other settings have also encountered constraints from their parent organizations and national health systems, alongside reported communication benefits. Implementing Buurtzorg-derived models in the home care setting: a Scoping Review

sections.title: What might explain it
sections.html:
Supported in case

Unchanged organizational approval systems can limit autonomy even when teams are described as self-managing. Transforming community nursing services in the UK: lessons from a participatory evaluation of the implementation of a new community nursing model in East London

Alternative explanation: Some retained controls may respond to statutory accountability or temporary implementation risks rather than simple resistance.

Plausible

Continuity may be a more transferable mechanism than the complete Dutch organizational structure. Transforming community nursing services in the UK: lessons from a participatory evaluation of the implementation of a new community nursing model in East London Implementing Buurtzorg-derived models in the home care setting: a Scoping Review

Alternative explanation: A small pilot with committed staff and favorable relationships may deliver attention that routine services cannot sustain.

sections.title: Questions to take into practice
sections.html:
• Specify which staffing, spending, and clinical decisions transfer before adopting a new team label.
  • Evaluate the adaptation against local aims and constraints, not only fidelity to an admired foreign model.

sections.title: What remains uncertain
sections.html:
• Could the pilot sustain staffing, continuity, and patient outcomes as it expanded?
  • How would total resource use compare with ordinary services once the support needed to establish the pilot was included?

title: Haier: markets and microenterprises inside a giant company
question: How much autonomy can small enterprises have within a large corporate platform?
summary: Haier reorganized parts of its business into small entrepreneurial units with substantial discretion over work, staffing, and remuneration. These units operate within a larger system of platforms, resources, and corporate direction. RenDanHeYi therefore combines decentralized enterprise activity with a powerful framework designer; it is not simply a collection of independent small businesses.
outcome_summary: Haier substantially redesigned its management, with different implementations across international businesses. By 2018 the newer microenterprise system was still young. Executives later associated it with growth and faster innovation, but acquisitions, investment, and market conditions also changed; the governance contribution is difficult to disentangle.

sections.title: What happened
sections.html:
Outcome evidence uncertain. Haier substantially redesigned its management, with different implementations across international businesses. By 2018 the newer microenterprise system was still young. Executives later associated it with growth and faster innovation, but acquisitions, investment, and market conditions also changed; the governance contribution is difficult to disentangle.

  • Small units gained discretion over recruitment and pay within a continuing corporate platform, with ownership stakes varying across arrangements. Management innovation made in China: Haier’s Rendanheyi
  • Overseas businesses adapted the model rather than implementing one uniform structure. The newer microenterprise arrangement was still developing in 2018. Management innovation made in China: Haier’s Rendanheyi
  • Zhang Ruimin described a long transition before performance improved and emphasized the continuing role of common principles and leadership. The Leader as Ecosystem Architect

sections.title: What might explain it
sections.html:
Participant explanation

Direct exposure to customer demand may help units test opportunities without routing every decision through a functional hierarchy. Management innovation made in China: Haier’s Rendanheyi The Leader as Ecosystem Architect

Alternative explanation: Industry demand, access to capital, distribution, and acquisitions may explain commercial results independently of the structure.

Plausible

Local autonomy may depend on centrally maintained interfaces and resources rather than a general retreat of leadership. Management innovation made in China: Haier’s Rendanheyi The Leader as Ecosystem Architect

Alternative explanation: Informal founder authority may resolve coordination problems that formal platform rules alone cannot handle.

sections.title: Understanding the outcome
sections.html:
Organizational modularity

Small units can experiment while shared platforms connect them. The Leader as Ecosystem Architect

When production dependencies are dense, a local experiment can disrupt other units; shared platforms still need ways to manage those connections.

sections.title: Questions to take into practice
sections.html:
• Distinguish a unit’s operating discretion, ownership, and exposure to financial losses.
  • Identify which shared services and integration decisions must remain reliable as units multiply.

sections.title: What remains uncertain
sections.html:
• How were income risk, unsuccessful units, and disputes handled within the microenterprise system?
  • Executive accounts leave workers’ experiences and unsuccessful transfers less visible than the intended advantages.

title: Morning Star: negotiating responsibilities with colleagues
question: Can explicit peer commitments replace routine supervisory assignment?
period: Practices documented in a 2018 field visit and company model
summary: At the tomato processor Morning Star, individual missions and agreements among colleagues define responsibilities between people whose activities depend on one another. These commitments replace routine assignment through a conventional supervisory chain. Coordination still requires negotiation, influence, and dispute resolution, even when job titles no longer identify a boss.
outcome_summary: The commitment system gave individuals substantial responsibility while requiring time to persuade colleagues and resolve disagreements. Favorable descriptions of that autonomy do not tell us how newcomers or dissatisfied employees experienced it, or whether the additional negotiation improved productivity enough to justify its cost.

sections.title: What happened
sections.html:
Outcome evidence uncertain. The commitment system gave individuals substantial responsibility while requiring time to persuade colleagues and resolve disagreements. Favorable descriptions of that autonomy do not tell us how newcomers or dissatisfied employees experienced it, or whether the additional negotiation improved productivity enough to justify its cost.

  • Colleague Letters of Understanding sit alongside personal, business-unit, and enterprise missions. Changes require affected colleagues’ knowledge and consent. Interactive Self-Management Model
  • During a 2018 plant visit, expertise-based influence operated alongside a staged disagreement process involving conversation, mediation, and peers. Building Great Teams: Hierarchy, self-management, scorecards, candour and coaching
  • Employees carried expanded responsibility and had to invest time in persuading colleagues instead of issuing orders. Building Great Teams: Hierarchy, self-management, scorecards, candour and coaching

sections.title: What might explain it
sections.html:
Plausible

Writing mutual commitments may make dependencies visible before missed work becomes a supervisory problem. Interactive Self-Management Model

Alternative explanation: Experienced colleagues and stable production routines may already coordinate effectively without a formal letter.

Supported in case

Removing routine command can shift coordination costs into negotiation rather than eliminate them. Building Great Teams: Hierarchy, self-management, scorecards, candour and coaching

Alternative explanation: Longer negotiation could be worthwhile if it produces better decisions; the balance between those gains and the time spent remains unclear.

sections.title: Questions to take into practice
sections.html:
• Clarify who can change a commitment and how disagreements move toward a decision.
  • Include coordination time when comparing self-management with conventional supervision.

sections.title: What remains uncertain
sections.html:
• What happened when colleagues repeatedly failed to agree, or when a newcomer had little influence?
  • Compensation decisions, ownership authority, and the experiences of people who left remain important to understanding how much power the agreements distributed.

title: Valve: choosing projects inside a company with owners
question: Does removing formal managers remove hierarchy or coordination bottlenecks?
summary: Valve’s 2012 employee handbook offered workers a choice of projects, opportunities to assemble teams, and peer assessment without a conventional managerial ladder. Initiative was unusually visible, but ownership, reputation, and influence remained consequential. A period of unfinished game projects raised a practical question: who sustains a shared priority when employees can choose where to work?
outcome_summary: Valve operated a distinctive project-selection and peer-evaluation system while retaining ownership authority and informal influence. Some game projects stalled before the eventual production of Half-Life: Alyx. Whether project choice caused those delays is contested: long development cycles, experimentation, and the company’s platform business could also explain the pattern.

sections.title: What happened
sections.html:
Mixed outcomes. Valve operated a distinctive project-selection and peer-evaluation system while retaining ownership authority and informal influence. Some game projects stalled before the eventual production of Half-Life: Alyx. Whether project choice caused those delays is contested: long development cycles, experimentation, and the company’s platform business could also explain the pattern.

  • The 2012 arrangement included self-selected projects and peer review, with comparative evaluations used in compensation. Valve Handbook for New Employees
  • Employee initiative coexisted with strategic authority tied to ownership and the judgment of influential people. Who’s the boss? The persistence of entrepreneurial hierarchy in flat organizations
  • Unfinished game projects preceded the eventual production of Half-Life: Alyx, creating pressure to explain how ambitious shared work was brought to completion. Who’s the boss? The persistence of entrepreneurial hierarchy in flat organizations

sections.title: What might explain it
sections.html:
Contested

Freedom to join appealing projects may leave difficult shared priorities under-resourced. Who’s the boss? The persistence of entrepreneurial hierarchy in flat organizations

Alternative explanation: Long game-development cycles, platform revenues, and deliberate experimentation could produce the same apparent output pattern.

Plausible

Peer assessment may replace managerial judgment with reputation-dependent influence rather than equal authority. Valve Handbook for New Employees Who’s the boss? The persistence of entrepreneurial hierarchy in flat organizations

Alternative explanation: Domain expertise can create legitimate differences in influence without an entrenched informal hierarchy.

sections.title: Understanding the outcome
sections.html:
Entrepreneurial judgment and persistent hierarchy

Someone still selects and sustains firm-wide commitments under uncertainty. Who’s the boss? The persistence of entrepreneurial hierarchy in flat organizations

Ownership gives a private company a particular source of strategic authority. A cooperative or voluntary association would have to locate that authority elsewhere.

sections.title: Questions to take into practice
sections.html:
• Ask who resolves conflicts between attractive projects and essential shared work.
  • Examine promotion, pay, and ownership alongside the formal organization chart.

sections.title: What remains uncertain
sections.html:
• How did employees with different reputations experience project choice, peer review, and pay decisions?
  • The 2012 handbook describes a historical arrangement; the extent to which those practices continued or changed is unclear.

title: Zappos: changing the rules and offering an exit
question: What can a forced governance transition reveal about consent and implementation?
summary: Zappos attempted to replace conventional management with Holacracy while its retail business continued operating. After a period of overlapping arrangements, Tony Hsieh announced a stronger transition and offered severance to employees who did not want to continue. The case exposes a tension between decentralizing day-to-day authority and using concentrated leadership power to impose the transition.
outcome_summary: Within a month of the 2015 severance offer, 14% of employees, including 20% of technology staff, departed. This concentrated disruption during an organizational transition, but the departures could reflect the package’s appeal as well as objections to the new rules. The immediate loss of staff and the long-term performance of Holacracy are separate questions.

sections.title: What happened
sections.html:
Mixed outcomes. Within a month of the 2015 severance offer, 14% of employees, including 20% of technology staff, departed. This concentrated disruption during an organizational transition, but the departures could reflect the package’s appeal as well as objections to the new rules. The immediate loss of staff and the long-term performance of Holacracy are separate questions.

  • Hsieh said overlapping legacy management and Holacracy were slowing change and set a deadline for removing people-manager roles. Zappos CEO Tony Hsieh: Adopt Holacracy Or Leave
  • Hsieh treated Holacracy as one tool within a broader ambition of self-management and offered transition support for former managers. Zappos CEO Tony Hsieh: Adopt Holacracy Or Leave
  • Departures following the severance offer included technology staff needed during an ongoing technology transition. Tony Hsieh at Zappos: Structure, Culture and Change

sections.title: What might explain it
sections.html:
Plausible

A decisive deadline may break organizational limbo but concentrate transition costs into a short period. Zappos CEO Tony Hsieh: Adopt Holacracy Or Leave Tony Hsieh at Zappos: Structure, Culture and Change

Alternative explanation: The severance package itself may attract departures independently of employees’ assessment of the governance model.

Plausible

Founder-driven decentralization can preserve founder power over the rules under which others gain autonomy. Zappos CEO Tony Hsieh: Adopt Holacracy Or Leave

Alternative explanation: An initial directive could establish lasting distributed authority rather than preserve founder control; the later distribution of power determines which interpretation fits.

sections.title: Questions to take into practice
sections.html:
• Separate adoption of a governance constitution from acceptance, work continuity, and long-term results.
  • Plan for loss of critical skills when offering an exit during a major redesign.

sections.title: What remains uncertain
sections.html:
• Why did employees leave, and how did their departures affect the work that remained?
  • Did distributed decision-making become durable after the founder-led transition, and what happened to operating performance?

title: FAVI: autonomy under customers and peers
question: Where does control go when a factory removes supervisory layers?
period: Reorganization from the late 1980s; studies published 2014 and 2017–2018
summary: FAVI organized production around customer-focused teams, giving workers substantial room to coordinate and improve daily work. Autonomy did not eliminate constraints: customer requirements, peer expectations, and leadership continued to shape what workers could do. Control moved partly into relationships with customers and colleagues.
outcome_summary: Workers participated in consequential production and team decisions while remaining subject to customer standards and pressure to fit their teams. Authority changed form rather than disappearing. Whether that change produced superior economic performance, and how its benefits and burdens were distributed among workers, remains uncertain.

sections.title: What happened
sections.html:
Mixed outcomes. Workers participated in consequential production and team decisions while remaining subject to customer standards and pressure to fit their teams. Authority changed form rather than disappearing. Whether that change produced superior economic performance, and how its benefits and burdens were distributed among workers, remains uncertain.

  • Customer-focused production units used coopted team leaders and combined operational, sales, and technical expertise. The liberated firm, a radical innovation or a mere avatar of participatory management?
  • Workers described pressure on newcomers to fit team expectations. Reduced supervision did not remove social sanctions. The liberated firm, a radical innovation or a mere avatar of participatory management?
  • Customer relationships shaped both procedures and informal expectations, influencing how the factory organized and controlled its work. Figures du client et management: un processus de structuration sous contrôle(s)

sections.title: What might explain it
sections.html:
Plausible

Closer contact with a customer may make priorities clearer without detailed instructions from a supervisor. Figures du client et management: un processus de structuration sous contrôle(s)

Alternative explanation: Stable contracts and customer-imposed standards may themselves provide much of the coordination.

Supported in case

Peer accountability may become coercive when fitting the group is necessary to remain employed. The liberated firm, a radical innovation or a mere avatar of participatory management?

Alternative explanation: Some peer expectations may protect reliability and shared work rather than enforce arbitrary conformity.

sections.title: Understanding the outcome
sections.html:
Social and bureaucratic control in customer–supplier relations

Trust-based relationships coexist with standards and monitoring rather than replacing them completely. Figures du client et management: un processus de structuration sous contrôle(s)

A supplier’s bargaining power and production dependencies affect how much a trusting customer relationship leaves room for autonomy.

sections.title: Questions to take into practice
sections.html:
• Map customer and peer constraints alongside formal reporting lines.
  • Ask how a newcomer can challenge a team norm without losing their place in the organization.

sections.title: What remains uncertain
sections.html:
• How did workers’ experiences change over time, particularly when teams struggled or customer demands tightened?
  • Would similar suppliers under comparable commercial pressure achieve the same results through different forms of supervision?

title: Semco: participation backed by business information
question: What makes employee discretion more than permission to give suggestions?
summary: Semco became a prominent example of participative management through employee involvement in work arrangements, supervisor selection, and business choices. Access to financial information and sharing financial results accompanied that discretion. The combination gave workers information and incentives to use their authority, rather than merely permission to offer suggestions.
