outcome_summary: Semco continued operating and grew commercially while expanding employee involvement. Semler and sympathetic observers attributed importance to the participative arrangements, but diversification, partnerships, economic conditions, and leadership also mattered. Commercial growth alone cannot reveal which of those changes contributed most.

sections.title: What happened
sections.html:
Outcome evidence uncertain. Semco continued operating and grew commercially while expanding employee involvement. Semler and sympathetic observers attributed importance to the participative arrangements, but diversification, partnerships, economic conditions, and leadership also mattered. Commercial growth alone cannot reveal which of those changes contributed most.

  • By 2005, employees had influence over work arrangements, supervisor selection, and business direction. Ricardo Semler Won’t Take Control
  • The company continued operating during Semler’s prolonged recovery after an accident. His temporary absence left ownership and previously established relationships intact. Ricardo Semler Won’t Take Control
  • Smaller business units combined participation with access to financial information and profit sharing. The Handy Guide to the Gurus of Management: Ricardo Semler

sections.title: What might explain it
sections.html:
Plausible

Sharing financial information may let local decisions reflect the economic consequences that managers otherwise interpret for workers. The Handy Guide to the Gurus of Management: Ricardo Semler

Alternative explanation: Financially skilled colleagues or informal leaders may still do most interpretation, limiting effective participation.

Plausible

Distributed operating knowledge may reduce dependence on the chief executive’s everyday availability. Ricardo Semler Won’t Take Control

Alternative explanation: A temporary absence leaves ownership, prior strategy, and trusted senior colleagues intact; permanent succession is a harder test.

sections.title: Understanding the outcome
sections.html:
McGregor’s Theory Y

The design assumes people can exercise responsibility when given information and meaningful discretion. Ricardo Semler Won’t Take Control

Responsibility depends on whether people can actually understand the information, influence consequential choices, and bear the risks of acting.

sections.title: Questions to take into practice
sections.html:
• Connect participation rights to usable information and the ability to act on it.
  • Test continuity during absence separately from ownership transfer or leadership succession.

sections.title: What remains uncertain
sections.html:
• How did employees who disliked the arrangements experience them, and how consistently were they used across different ventures?
  • The accounts concern the 1980s through 2005; later changes may have altered both participation and leadership dependence.

title: GitLab: written context with one accountable decision-maker
question: How can a distributed team combine wide input with clear decisions?
summary: GitLab combines durable written context with a named person responsible for a decision. Its handbook asks workers to update documentation when practices change, while a directly responsible individual seeks relevant input and then decides. This pairs accessible organizational memory with differentiated authority in a company whose workers cannot rely on being in the same room.
outcome_summary: GitLab makes decision ownership and documentation procedures publicly inspectable. Writing a durable update can initially take longer than sending a message, creating a recurring tension between immediate convenience and future usefulness. The written rules show how the arrangement is intended to work; how consistently people follow them and whether they save time overall remain open questions.

sections.title: What happened
sections.html:
Outcome evidence uncertain. GitLab makes decision ownership and documentation procedures publicly inspectable. Writing a durable update can initially take longer than sending a message, creating a recurring tension between immediate convenience and future usefulness. The written rules show how the arrangement is intended to work; how consistently people follow them and whether they save time overall remain open questions.

  • A directly responsible individual consults stakeholders but holds ultimate responsibility for the decision without needing everyone’s agreement. Directly Responsible Individuals (DRIs)
  • The proposed workflow connects issues, edits, merging, and announcements so a changed practice has a durable written location. Handbook usage
  • Quicker conversations can bypass the handbook, so keeping the shared record current requires continuing effort. Handbook usage

sections.title: What might explain it
sections.html:
Plausible

A named decision owner can prevent consultation from becoming an unresolved demand for unanimity. Directly Responsible Individuals (DRIs)

Alternative explanation: If relevant knowledge is missed or authority is mistrusted, a faster decision may simply move conflict downstream.

Participant explanation

Updating shared context at the time of change may reduce repeated explanation across locations and time zones. Handbook usage

Alternative explanation: The benefit depends on discoverability and reading habits; a large stale handbook could instead increase search costs.

sections.title: Questions to take into practice
sections.html:
• Document who decides, who must be consulted, and where the final decision lives.
  • Treat documentation maintenance as work with owners rather than an optional cleanup activity.

sections.title: What remains uncertain
sections.html:
• When decisions are contested, how much influence do consultation and the named decision owner each carry?
  • How often does documentation become stale, and who bears the effort of finding and repairing it?

title: Loomio: different rooms have different decision rights
question: What must an online discussion space specify before its decisions mean anything?
period: Handbook mainly circa 2016; explicit archive update in 2022
summary: Loomio is both decision-making software and a worker cooperative that uses it. Its archived handbook distinguishes spaces for co-owners, workers, directors, and public contributors, with different kinds of authority. The example shows how participation software depends on social agreements about membership, facilitation, privacy, and the consequences of a vote.
outcome_summary: Loomio’s earlier arrangement separated binding decisions from advice and gave working groups a route to escalate matters beyond their mandates. The cooperative later became smaller and changed its practices; the circa-2016 rules describe that earlier design, not its current procedures. Their practical effect on disputed decisions and participation remains unclear.

sections.title: What happened
sections.html:
Outcome evidence uncertain. Loomio’s earlier arrangement separated binding decisions from advice and gave working groups a route to escalate matters beyond their mandates. The cooperative later became smaller and changed its practices; the circa-2016 rules describe that earlier design, not its current procedures. Their practical effect on disputed decisions and participation remains unclear.

  • Each online group was expected to specify its purpose, membership, facilitation, privacy, and the meaning of its decisions. Loomio Using Loomio
  • Co-owner, worker, and board spaces held different binding powers; public groups could be advisory or lack decision authority. Working groups could escalate decisions beyond their mandates. Loomio Using Loomio
  • By 2022, the operational team was smaller, and many procedures preserved in the handbook belonged to an earlier phase. Loomio Cooperative Handbook: Introduction

sections.title: What might explain it
sections.html:
Plausible

Explicitly distinguishing recommendations from binding decisions may prevent apparent participation from creating false expectations. Loomio Using Loomio

Alternative explanation: Participants may still infer authority from visibility or status unless the distinction is repeatedly explained.

Participant explanation

Persistent discussion can include colleagues absent from a particular meeting, but participation still needs active facilitation. Loomio Using Loomio

Alternative explanation: Digital access and available attention may reproduce exclusion even when conversations remain open longer.

sections.title: Questions to take into practice
sections.html:
• Label who a discussion includes and what authority its eventual result carries.
  • Give small working groups a path for escalating decisions beyond their mandate.

sections.title: What remains uncertain
sections.html:
• How did participants resolve disputes about which group had authority?
  • Which members participated consistently, and how did the later reduction in team size change decision-making?

title: Occupy Wall Street: the assembly and the time it consumes
question: When does open participation need smaller delegated structures?
period: New York occupation in 2011 and subsequent organizing
location: Zuccotti Park, New York City, United States
summary: Occupy Wall Street made a general assembly central to its political practice, using modified consensus and public discussion. Working groups carried out practical tasks, and organizers later introduced a spokescouncil to coordinate them. This was both a way to organize a protest and an attempt to enact the more participatory society participants wanted.
outcome_summary: The occupation created solidarity, participation, and a visible alternative political culture while also encountering long meetings, obstruction, and unequal ability to spend time in deliberation. Introducing a spokescouncil changed how working groups coordinated. Police eviction sharply interrupted the experiment, so organizational difficulties alone do not explain its end.

sections.title: What happened
sections.html:
Mixed outcomes. The occupation created solidarity, participation, and a visible alternative political culture while also encountering long meetings, obstruction, and unequal ability to spend time in deliberation. Introducing a spokescouncil changed how working groups coordinated. Police eviction sharply interrupted the experiment, so organizational difficulties alone do not explain its end.

  • Modified consensus included a high-threshold fallback when a proposal remained blocked, rather than requiring unanimous approval in every instance. What the Left Can Learn from Occupy Wall Street
  • Meeting duration and disruption became problems, and a spokescouncil was approved in late October 2011. What the Left Can Learn from Occupy Wall Street
  • Assemblies and collective life drew on earlier radical traditions. Eviction ended the occupation of the site, interrupting the development of its institutions. The Occupy Wall Street Movement in the American Radical Tradition

sections.title: What might explain it
sections.html:
Contested

Direct participation may strengthen commitment among people sharing the risks of an occupation. What the Left Can Learn from Occupy Wall Street

Alternative explanation: Shared danger, material support, and the emotional force of protest may generate solidarity independently of consensus rules.

Supported in case

An open meeting can give disproportionate influence to people with abundant time. What the Left Can Learn from Occupy Wall Street

Alternative explanation: Speaking norms, facilitation skill, and existing social status may matter as much as time availability.

sections.title: Understanding the outcome
sections.html:
Prefigurative politics

Organizing practices are intended to embody desired social relations in the present. The Occupy Wall Street Movement in the American Radical Tradition

Experiencing a different political relationship does not by itself establish durable institutional capacity or broader policy change.

sections.title: Questions to take into practice
sections.html:
• Measure the time cost of participation and who cannot afford it.
  • Distinguish decisions needing a whole assembly from work that can be delegated with accountability.

sections.title: What remains uncertain
sections.html:
• Whose participation diminished as meetings lengthened, and did the spokescouncil change that pattern?
  • Which relationships and organizing capacities survived the eviction? New York’s trajectory was only one part of the wider Occupy movement.

title: Alcoholics Anonymous: local groups and shared traditions
question: What does evidence for a peer fellowship tell us about its governance?
period: Traditions endorsed in 1950; treatment evidence reviewed in 2020
location: International fellowship; research largely in the United States
summary: Alcoholics Anonymous combines local peer groups with shared traditions concerning autonomy, service, anonymity, and financial independence. Local groups have room to organize their activities while remaining connected to a recognizable fellowship. Professional Twelve-Step Facilitation can help people engage with AA, but its clinical effects answer a different question from how the fellowship distributes authority.
outcome_summary: For adults with alcohol use disorder, a 2020 Cochrane review found strong evidence that manualized AA/Twelve-Step Facilitation improved continuous abstinence compared with some established alternatives, while other outcomes were often similar. That result concerns a defined route into participation, not a guarantee about any meeting or person. It also leaves open which organizational practices contributed to the benefit.

sections.title: What happened
sections.html:
Mixed outcomes. For adults with alcohol use disorder, a 2020 Cochrane review found strong evidence that manualized AA/Twelve-Step Facilitation improved continuous abstinence compared with some established alternatives, while other outcomes were often similar. That result concerns a defined route into participation, not a guarantee about any meeting or person. It also leaves open which organizational practices contributed to the benefit.

  • Shared traditions allow local autonomy within limits concerning other groups, place leaders in service to their groups, and call for financial self-support. 12 Traditions
  • Accountable service boards and employed specialist workers support the fellowship. Local autonomy and nonprofessional peer relationships coexist with organizational infrastructure. 12 Traditions
  • Clinical comparisons differed in their facilitation methods, alternatives, and measured outcomes. The strongest abstinence finding concerned structured, manualized AA/Twelve-Step Facilitation. Alcoholics Anonymous (AA) and other 12-step programs for alcohol use disorder

sections.title: What might explain it
sections.html:
Plausible

Shared traditions may help local groups reproduce a recognizable practice without requiring detailed central administration. 12 Traditions

Alternative explanation: Informal norms, literature, and experienced members may do more coordinating work than formal statements alone.

Plausible

Peer relationships may help sustain participation, but the outcome evidence does not identify governance as the mechanism. Alcoholics Anonymous (AA) and other 12-step programs for alcohol use disorder

Alternative explanation: Professional facilitation, motivation, social-network change, and selection into attendance may contribute in different combinations.

sections.title: Questions to take into practice
sections.html:
• Separate evidence for participation or facilitation from evidence for particular organizational rules.
  • Study service infrastructure and local accountability alongside the rhetoric of autonomy.

sections.title: What remains uncertain
sections.html:
• How do differences in local governance affect participation, accountability, and experiences of exclusion?
  • The clinical findings principally concern noncoerced treatment contexts for adults with alcohol use disorder; whether similar organizational arrangements help unrelated peer groups is a separate question.

title: Guerrilla Translation and DisCO: making care visible in the accounts
question: Can a collective pay for commons work without ignoring the work of maintaining itself?
period: Guerrilla Translation/Media Collective model, redesigned in 2018; later DisCO documentation
summary: Guerrilla Translation and the wider Guerrilla Media Collective provided an early setting for DisCO governance. Their model distinguishes paid client work, freely shared translations, and the care and administration that sustain the collective. Contribution accounting and income allocation are intended to connect these activities, with membership commitments determining participation in binding decisions.
outcome_summary: The collective developed and revised a governance model that connects commercial income, freely shared translations, and the care required to maintain the group. The accounting makes those commitments visible, but a recorded contribution is not cash in hand. Whether the arrangement consistently financed unpaid work or reduced unequal burdens remains unclear.

sections.title: What happened
sections.html:
Outcome evidence uncertain. The collective developed and revised a governance model that connects commercial income, freely shared translations, and the care required to maintain the group. The accounting makes those commitments visible, but a recorded contribution is not cash in hand. Whether the arrangement consistently financed unpaid work or reduced unequal burdens remains unclear.

  • The model distinguishes livelihood, pro-bono, and care work, giving them different accounting treatment and linking participation rights to membership commitments. Distributed Cooperative Organization (DisCO) Governance Model V 3.0
  • Guerrilla Media Collective became the first DisCO Lab and collaboratively redesigned its arrangements in 2018. Groove is in the Heart: The DisCO Elements
  • One version directs a defined share of available income toward previously recorded pro-bono contributions. The allocation rules can be revised as circumstances change. Groove is in the Heart: The DisCO Elements

sections.title: What might explain it
sections.html:
Participant explanation

Recording maintenance and relational work may make unequal burdens discussable before they become invisible obligations. Distributed Cooperative Organization (DisCO) Governance Model V 3.0

Alternative explanation: Tracking can become another administrative burden, while the people doing care may still lack bargaining power.

Participant explanation

Reserving income for commons contributions may sustain work that clients would not directly buy. Groove is in the Heart: The DisCO Elements

Alternative explanation: The arrangement depends on adequate paid demand; accounting recognition cannot itself create money or guarantee timely payment.

sections.title: Understanding the outcome
sections.html:
Feminist economics and recognition of reproductive work

The model treats sustaining people and the collective as economically relevant activity. Groove is in the Heart: The DisCO Elements

Recording care leaves difficult choices about its value, who judges it, and whether enough income exists to compensate the people doing it.

sections.title: Questions to take into practice
sections.html:
• Distinguish recognition of a contribution from cash actually available to compensate it.
  • Track the cost of accounting and who decides what counts as care.

sections.title: What remains uncertain
sections.html:
• How long did recorded contributions remain unpaid, and what happened when members left or disputed their balances?
  • Did tracking care redistribute its burden, or mainly give existing work a more visible record?

title: ElderSpirit: choosing neighbors and organizing help
question: How can a neighborhood make mutual support dependable without promising unlimited care?
period: Initial research published 2009; follow-up published 2013; current community guidance
summary: ElderSpirit is an intentional elder cohousing community where residents organize shared life and neighborly assistance. Its support system asks a member to identify two coordinators who can help arrange practical assistance when needed. The case makes the social infrastructure of friendship concrete while explicitly distinguishing independent living and volunteer help from an assisted-living service.
outcome_summary: Residents described valued interdependence, comfort, and mutual support after an initially demanding period of community building. The early group was small and self-selected, with a narrow demographic composition. Its experience therefore leaves open how accessible the arrangement would be to people with different resources and needs. Volunteer support also had limits: some residents needed outside help or a different living arrangement.

sections.title: What happened
sections.html:
Mixed outcomes. Residents described valued interdependence, comfort, and mutual support after an initially demanding period of community building. The early group was small and self-selected, with a narrow demographic composition. Its experience therefore leaves open how accessible the arrangement would be to people with different resources and needs. Volunteer support also had limits: some residents needed outside help or a different living arrangement.

  • The 33 charter residents studied in 2009 were all white and mostly women. They had actively chosen the community, with mutual support an important motivation. Aging in a Community of Mutual Support: The Emergence of an Elder Intentional Cohousing Community in the United States
  • Residents later described improvement after the initial setup work, alongside disputes about participation, privacy concerns, and physical-design barriers. Lessons Learned From a New Elder Cohousing Community
  • Members identify two neighborly support coordinators to help arrange short-term practical assistance. The arrangement has limits when independent living is no longer feasible. Mutual Support

sections.title: What might explain it
sections.html:
Plausible

Named coordinators may lower the effort required to ask for help and distribute requests among neighbors. Mutual Support

Alternative explanation: Pre-existing relationships and residents’ willingness to help may matter more than the coordinator role itself.

Plausible

An initially difficult formation period may build the agreements that make later cooperation easier. Lessons Learned From a New Elder Cohousing Community

Alternative explanation: Adaptation, selective departures, or changing expectations could also explain more favorable later reports.

sections.title: Questions to take into practice
sections.html:
• Agree on practical help, responsibility for coordinating it, and limits before a crisis occurs.
  • Budget time for building community agreements rather than assuming shared housing produces support automatically.

sections.title: What remains uncertain
sections.html:
• What happened to people who left, and how evenly did remaining neighbors share the care work?
  • Could people with fewer resources or different access needs obtain comparable support?
  • The early accounts came from a self-selected group and a researcher previously involved in community planning, leaving dissatisfied and outside perspectives less visible.
